You will see a list of every story you’ve created, including view and reaction counts for each.

Can I delete or edit a story once it is shared?

To delete a story, press the 3 Vertical Dots menu icon on the top-right of your stories, and select Delete.

If you delete a story after it’s been shared, it will no longer be available to view by anyone. This includes seeing the story in your history.

What happens to my story if an emote is deleted?
If an emote used in a story is removed from Twitch (whether by you or by Twitch), all stories that use that emote will also be removed.
Can a user I’ve banned or blocked from my channel see my story?
No. If a viewer is banned or blocked from your channel, they cannot see your story on their Stories shelf.
What if my story fails to post?
  • You may have uploaded an image that is outside of our file limits
  • You may have uploaded an image that is not one of our accepted file formats.
  • Your internet connection may not be strong enough to complete the post
  • You may have attempted to post a story that violates Twitch’s Terms of Service or Community Guidelines.
What emotes can be used in stories?
You can add global Twitch emotes and your own channel’s emotes to your stories. Earned emotes from other channels or some campaigns are not available. Of course you can also use the entire library of emoji you have in your mobile keyboard in any text field.
How will I know if I am mentioned in a story?
You will receive an onsite message and a push notification if you are mentioned by another channel.
How can I opt-out of being mentioned in others’ stories?
Within “Security and Privacy” in account Settings there is a ‘Mentions in Stories’ setting. You can change who can mention you in a story via this setting. If a channel is suspended or banned by Twitch, they cannot be mentioned. If you block or ban a channel, that channel cannot mention you in their stories.
Why was my story muted?
Your story may be muted if copyright audio is detected and you may be notified of this change.

Stream Together

Stream Together is a native feature of the Twitch streaming experience available to anyone with a Twitch account, regardless of monetization status. Stream Together enables collaboration on-stream with other streamers across multiple live channels, or as guests on a single channel. Collaborating on Twitch is both fun and valuable - it helps build bonds with other streamers and showcases your personality and channel to their communities. Stream Together also makes it easy for streamers to bring members of their community live on stream, which can help strengthen your community and reward your valued community members.

A collaboration is when you team up live with other streamers on Twitch. When you start a collaboration, you choose what to share: Shared Chat (combine your chats, which also combines your view counts with Shared Viewership and lets you run a Shared Hype Train), Audio/Video (join a Stream Together call so you can see and hear each other on stream), or both. This article covers Audio/Video. For Shared Chat, see Shared Chat.

About Stream Together

Stream Together is a Twitch feature that works with broadcast software like OBS or Streamlabs OBS to make it easy for streamers to collaborate live on-stream with streamers or viewers. Stream Together is currently in Beta. During the Beta, give us feedback on how the tool can be even greater for Twitch creators and their communities.

Befre we dive in, these definitions will help you navigate these instructions:

  • Host - The streamer who creates and manages the Stream Together call
  • Guest - A streamer invited by the Host to join the Stream Together call
  • Streaming Collaborator - Guests of a Host who are also streaming to their channel while participating in a Stream Together call

Because Stream Together is still in Beta, currently only certain broadcasting software and web browsers are supported. More browsers and broadcasting software will be supported in the future.

Requirements

All Twitch users have access to Stream Together. While there are no system requirements to view streams using Stream Together, Hosts and streaming collaborators need a few things before they can start a call, or join a call while streaming.

To create a Stream Together call, Hosts need:

  • Broadcasting software (such as OBS or Streamlabs OBS)
  • A web browser (such as Google Chrome)

Streaming Collaborators need both Twitch in a web browser, and broadcasting software to stream to their channels while joining a Stream Together call.

To join a Stream Together call without streaming, Guests need:

  • A web browser to join the call from twitch.tv, or
  • The Twitch Mobile App

For security purposes, Guests who are not Affiliates or Partners need to add a verified phone number to their accounts.

Getting Started

Before you begin, make sure you meet the requirements listed above.

To start a Stream Together call:

  • Go to the Stream Together tab of your Creator Dashboard, or the Collaboration panel in your Stream Manager, and click Invite to Collaborate.
  • In the Invite and Start a Collaboration window, check Audio/Video. Check Shared Chat too if you also want to combine your chats.
  • Choose who to invite, then click Send Invite. The Stream Together window opens right away.

You can also Copy Browser Source URL from the Stream Together tab of your Creator Dashboard.

Setting Up Audio

If this is your first time setting up Stream Together, your browser will request microphone access. Once you have granted access, select a device to use with Stream Together.

By default, Stream Together call audio comes from your browser and is captured in Desktop Audio. You’ll want to ensure audio captured from Stream Together is heard on your stream. Here are a few options:

  • Make sure your streaming software is capturing Desktop Audio
  • Change the audio output of Stream Together to a different device in your Settings (and make sure your streaming software is accepting audio from that device)
  • Route the audio through the video browser sources, a process described in this article’s section Showing the Call on Your Stream.

You can access and update your microphone input and audio output settings by clicking on Settings .

For help with audio issues, please see Troubleshooting Audio.

Setting Up Video

To add your own video feed to your Stream Together call, enable by clicking the video button in the bottom bar. Once you make this selection, your browser will ask permission to capture video. Giving the browser access allows you to select a video device for your Stream Together call.

For help with audio issues, please see Troubleshooting Video.

Virtual Camera

If your device is unselectable or not visible, you may need to set up a Virtual Camera. This is common on PCs, where each video device can only be utilized once. If your streaming software is using your camera as a video capture input, it won’t appear to be available in Stream Together. Luckily, there is a simple fix:

In OBS Version 28 or later:

  • Click Start Virtual Camera button in main OBS control area
  • Select Virtual Camera Settings
  • Select Source under Output Type
  • Select your desired Video Capture Device under Output Selection

In Streamlabs OBS:

  • Go to Settings, then Virtual Webcam
  • Click Install Virtual Webcam
  • Click Start Virtual Webcam
  • The virtual camera will capture the active scene in Streamlabs, and that will be what the output of the virtual camera. Because of this, your virtual camera output will be of what you are streaming, not just your traditional camera (face cam, vtuber model, etc)

Once these steps are complete, you should see the virtual camera as a selectable video device in Stream Together and can use it in a call.

Each time you want to use a virtual camera, you need to start it in your streaming software.

For more information on virtual cameras, visit our help guide About Virtual Cameras

Showing the Call on Your Stream

Stream Together enables you to show your call on your live stream through the use of browser sources in your streaming software. You only need to set up the browser sources once, and they will continue to work for any Stream Together call you join.

Browser sources connect web browsers to your streaming software through a link (URL). Stream Together uses these browser source links to display the video feeds from your call on your stream.

There are two separate approaches to display your video feeds on your stream. Which to use depends on the needs of your setup.

  • Group Capture Browser Source unifies all participant feeds into a single source
  • Individual Browser Sources allow you to manually place each call participant on your screen.
Group Capture Browser Source

If you’re familiar with Zoom or Google Meets, Group Capture is the easiest way to use Stream Together. Imagine you want to stream reaction content with your friends. A single Group Capture browser source enables everyone’s camera to dynamically shift around a screenshare of the reaction content.

All call participants are shown on stream via the same browser source. Group Browser Source automatically adjusts when guests leave or join the call, and responds to whatever layout you choose.

Beneath participant videos are different layout options. Participant videos automatically move and resize when you select different layouts.

Many streamers use separate video feeds for their streams. So, by default, Stream Together does not include your own camera in your browser source output. You can change this setting by toggling on “include camera in group output.”

Individual Browser Sources

Use Individual Browser Sources for more control over your layout. More setup is required, but this video capture method enables the most customization within your streaming software. For example, if you are streaming a co-op game with friends, using individual browser sources allows you to place each player camera near their game stats or player info.

With this approach, each participant’s video feed is sent via their own individual browser source. This allows you to place, resize, and manipulate each video feed one-by-one in your scene as you wish. You can do the same for your own camera feed.

Adding Your Browser Sources to Your Streaming Software

Now that your browser sources are set in your streaming software scene the way you like, they will continue to work every time you use Stream Together. You do not need to set up Stream Together each time you collaborate, unless you wish to make changes to your layout.

To add the browser sources to your streaming software for the first time, you’ll need to locate your Browser Source Link(s) in Stream Together. To do so, in Stream Together:

  • Visit Settings->Browser Sources. You will see a list of labeled obfuscated links.
  • Click Copy on a link that you want to add into your streaming software

Next, turn to your streaming software:

  • Create a New Browser Source in your preferred scene
  • Paste your link in the text entry box

That’s it! After this, you can add more individual browser sources for each Stream Together guest using the same steps. Or, you can resize the Stream Together video, finish adjusting your overlay, and get ready to stream.

Stream Together videos default to 1920 width x 1080 height. We recommend manually entering a size of 800 width x 600 height.

If your browser source links get exposed or leaked, regenerate them in your Browser Source Settings by scrolling to the bottom and clicking Regenerate

To learn more about browser sources and streaming software, visit our friends at OBS.

Inviting People to Collaborate

Congratulations, you’ve set up Stream Together! Now, it’s time to collaborate. You can bring guests into your Stream Together call through multiple ways, which are described below. Your guests can also bring other guests into the call. Guests who choose to stream while in the call become streaming collaborators. Collaboration settings for your channel only apply to users attempting to knock on your channel, all other invite methods bypass these settings.

Inviting People Directly

To directly invite specific Guests to a Stream Together call, follow these steps:

  • Click Invite Guests in your Stream Together call, or Invite to Collaborate in the Collaboration panel in your Stream Manager
  • Search for users or choose them from pre-built tabs that show your favorites, subscribers, recents, etc. Click on as many users as you want to invite.
  • Click Send Invites
Inviting People With an Invite Link

You can also send anyone an invite link – for example through a messaging platform, email, or text – which will directly let them into the call after they sign into Twitch. To use an invite link, follow these steps:

  • Click the Invite Guests button from a Stream Together call
  • At the bottom of the invite window, there is an obfuscated invite link
  • Click the Copy button next to the invite link
  • Send the invite link directly via messaging to the person you want to bring into the call.

If a user is blocked or banned by you or anyone else in the call, they will not be able to access the call through an invite link.

Important: If your invite links get exposed or leaked, regenerate them in the Invite Guests window by scrolling to the bottom and clicking the Regenerate icon

Inviting People From Chat

While streaming, you are able to directly invite a chatter to a Stream Together call through the following steps:

  • Click on a chatter’s name
  • Click on the purple Invite button (next to Follow and Whisper)
Opening a Request Line

While streaming you can open up a request line to let your viewers raise their hand and ask to join you on stream. Requests lines are a unique way to engage with your community and can add exciting moments of appreciation for your community members. You can restrict who is able to join the request line (for example subs of 6+ months), and you can hand pick who from the request line you want to invite up.

To open a request line, use the following steps:

  • Start a Stream Together call (see Getting Started)
  • Click on the Requests button in your Stream Together call
  • Choose who you want to be able to request to join. You can even limit by follower or sub length, and if you want them to be audio-only
  • Click Start Requests
  • Viewers on your stream can raise their hands and they will show up in your request line
  • Click Add to Call to invite a viewer into the call
  • If they accept the invite, they will join the call
Knock on Streams and Ask to Drop In

We recently introduced new capabilities that make it easier than ever to collaborate spontaneously on Twitch. You can set your collaboration status which determines what users are able to knock and drop in on your stream when you’re live.

When someone knocks on your stream, you will see a notification in chat. If you accept the request, a Stream Together call will open and they will receive an invite to the call.

Learn more about collaborations and how to manage them here.

Once a guest has accepted an invitation, they will join the call. They may need to set up their microphone if this is their first time using Stream Together, so you may not hear them right away. To learn more about quick first time setup, check out this article.

Collaboration Features

Stream Together is designed to make collaborations seamless and engaging. When using Stream Together for collaborations, hosts of the call can allow other participants to show the call on their own streams. This is enabled by default.

When enabled, the other participants will be able to see the video feeds from the call in their own browser source links used in their own streaming software. They can choose their own layouts and can choose their own placements of the video feeds.

Hosts of a call can manage collaboration settings at any time by going into Settings->Browser Sources and toggling Allow Streaming Collaborators to Stream Your Call.

Collaboration features help create shared experiences where multiple streamers can work together while maintaining control over their individual streams and audiences.

Settings

You can access Stream Together settings anytime by clicking the Settings icon in the call controls (at the bottom of the call). Within Settings, there are 8 tabs

Browser Sources:

In this tab, you have access to all your browser source URLs, as well as your collaboration settings.

To learn more about the different browser source URLs, learn more about Browser Sources.

At the bottom of this settings tab, you can regenerate your browser source URLs. You will want to do this in case any of your links are shown on stream, sent to others, or leaked. Once you have regenerated your URLs, you will need to update your browser sources in your streaming software to use the new URLs.

Camera

In this tab you have access to your camera device. If you are having trouble accessing your camera in Stream Together, you may need to use a Virtual Camera. Check out this article to learn more.

Microphone

In this tab you have access to your microphone device as well as your audio input settings. The audio input settings available are:

  • Automatically determine input gain: Let Twitch manually determine your input sensitivity or control it yourself
  • Noise Suppression: removes unwanted sounds from your surroundings
  • Echo Cancellation: prevents speaker sounds from creating an echo effect
Audio Output

In this tab, you can change the output device that Stream Together sends audio to as well as update your browser source audio settings. There are two options for how browser source audio works:

  • Output Volume: The overall volume of the call, separate from your computer’s volume.
  • Desktop Audio Capture: This is the default and recommended setting. This mutes your browser sources and does not send call audio to your streaming software. If you are capturing Desktop audio in your streaming software, this is the setting you want, otherwise you will get doubled audio.
  • Control via Streaming Software: This option sends the call audio through your browser sources into your streaming software, and you can control the audio in your streaming softwares audio mixer. The call audio still comes through your desktop audio with this option.

For more help with audio, check out our tips on Troubleshooting Audio

Moderator

This tab is where you can set your Stream Together mods. Stream Together mods can only be selected from your current channel mods.

Stream Together mods can take actions like inviting guests, reporting guests, removing guests, muting guests, and turning off guests video.

Stream Together Mods do not need to be invited to a Stream Together call to have access to the call. They can access the call through your link, which is provided at the top of the Moderator Settings tab. They can also access it through your channels mod view. Stream Together mods must be on desktop to moderate the call.

Nameplates

In this tab, you can customize the look of the nameplates that are shown over the video feeds in Stream Together.

You can choose between the sizes of small, medium, and large.

You can also choose the location among a predetermined selection of options.

Performance

In this tab, you can access settings that will help with the performance of your Stream Together call. You can turn these mitigation settings on at any time, but Stream Together will also automatically enable these settings when it detects you are having performance issues.

The performance settings include:

  • Hide Video Preview: hides video backstage to reduce memory consumption. Videos are still visible in your browser sources.
  • Video Quality: adjust the maximum quality of the video you send to Stream Together to reduce CPU usage. This will effect how others see your video and how it appears in browser sources.

If you are still experiencing performance issues, such as choppy/freezing video, dropped audio, etc, please click the ! icon in the top right and file a feedback report to our team and indicate what kind of performance issues you are experiencing- this helps our team diagnose the issues and improve Stream Together.

Safety

You are not penalized for other user’s behavior

Because Stream Together is built directly into Twitch, each call participant is responsible for their own behavior, and reports can be made against their Twitch account. Please note though that while guests can be reported and will receive penalties (even if the infraction was shown on the host’s stream), the host does need to condemn the behavior and remove that offending guest from the call.

*** As long as a host takes proper actions to condemn and remove misbehaving guests from the call, hosts will not be penalized for the guests behavior***

Reporting Call Participants

There are multiple places to report guests who are misbehaving:

  • Channel Page: On the channel page of a livestream that is participating in the call, call participants will be listed in the reporting dropdown
  • Backstage user controls: In Stream Together backstage, you can click on the three dot dropdown menu for any guest and report them
  • Backstage recent guests: In Stream Together backstage, there is a dropdown where hosts can see recent guests and can report them
  • Call exit screen: When a guest is kicked out of a call, they can report the host if needed.

Troubleshooting Audio

To learn more about setting up audio, see the Setting Up Audio section of this page. Below are some problems you may encounter with audio and how to resolve them:

Echo/Tinny Audio on Stream

If you are hearing tinny/echoing audio in your stream, this may be because your broadcasting software is receiving Stream Together audio through Chrome/Desktop Audio and the browser source for your guests at the same time. To fix this, click on the Settings cog icon in the bottom of your Stream Together backstage window and select Audio Output and make sure Desktop Audio Capture is the option selected

Can’t Hear the Call on Stream

If you cannot hear your guests on stream, check your Browser Source Audio Settings to see where you are outputting audio. If you have Desktop Audio selected, make sure that you are capturing desktop audio in your streaming software. If you selected Control Audio via Streaming Software, check your audio mixer in your streaming software and check if it is receiving audio. If not, check to make sure that the source is not muted in the audio mixer.

Volume of Participants or Myself is Wrong

If the volume of your mic or your participants’ outputs are wrong, you can adjust them in a few places.

To adjust the input level of your own mic, go to Settings -> Microphone where you can adjust if you or Twitch handles your input, and adjust the input sensitivity manually if needed. You can also test your mic’s input levels on this page.

To adjust the output volume of the call, go to Settings-> Audio Output where you can raise or lower the volume as needed.

To adjust a single call participant’s volume, you can click on the three dot dropdown next to their name in the right panel of the call, where you will then see a volume slider. Adjusting this slider affects only this participant’s audio for you.

Can’t Hear the Call on VODs

If this is happening to you, you most likely have previously configured your streaming software audio settings to keep certain audio sources out of your VODs. You can check your configuration in the Output tab of your OBS settings. Make sure the audio source that contains Stream Together is routing to both your primary Audio Track and your Twitch VOD Track. Settings for individual audio sources can be found within the Advanced Audio Properties menu in OBS.

Enabled my Camera in Group Capture and Now Hear Myself Twice

If you have your browser source audio output set to Control Audio via Streaming Software and then you enabled your camera in group capture, your feed in the group capture is sending your microphone into the browser source audio which is causing doubling on your stream. To fix this, click on the Settings cog icon in the bottom of your Stream Together backstage window and click on Audio Output. Underneath the Control via Streaming Software setting you will see a toggle for send audio with your camera via Browser Source. Turn this toggle off.

Troubleshooting Video

A common issue streamers have is Windows device exclusivity, which makes it so Stream Together/other applications can’t access a camera that is already in use by another application, this usually being your streaming software. If you are experiencing this issue, please see our dedicated article on virtual cameras which will walk you through how to resolve this issue in both OBS and Streamlabs OBS.

Troubleshooting Performance

There are a few possible reasons you may be experiencing performance issues in Stream Together, the most common being network issues, with the next two being CPU usage and Memory usage.

Stream Together does automatic performance degradation detecting during your call and will automatically trigger performance saving settings in an attempt to help.You may notice these alerts at the bottom of your call. If you wish to manually turn on these settings, navigate to the Performance tab of your Settings.

The performance settings include:

  • Hide Video Preview: hides video backstage to reduce memory consumption. Videos are still visible in your browser sources.
  • Video Quality: adjust the maximum quality of the video you send to Stream Together to reduce CPU usage. This will affect how others see your video and how it appears in browser sources.

If you are still experiencing performance issues, please click the ! icon in the top right of the Stream Together window and file a feedback report to our team and indicate what kind of performance issues you are experiencing- this helps our team diagnose the issues and improve Stream Together.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Stream Together work on Mobile?
You can join Stream Together calls from a mobile device, but you cannot host a Stream Together calls from a mobile device.

Stream Together Troubleshooting Guide

When Stream Together isn’t performing optimally, you might notice several issues during your stream. This guide will help you identify common problems and provide step-by-step solutions to improve your streaming experience.

Understanding Performance Issues

When Stream Together isn’t performing optimally, you might notice several telltale signs during your stream. Let’s break down what you might experience and why it happens.

What You Might Experience
  • OBS Crashes: Your streaming software suddenly closes or becomes unresponsive
  • Laggy Camera Feeds: Your video (or your collaborator’s) appears frozen or delayed
  • Audio Problems: Sound becomes choppy, robotic, or out of sync
  • High CPU Usage: Your computer slows down or your fans start working overtime
  • Browser Source Issues: Stream Together video feeds freeze in OBS
Why This Happens

Your PC is already working hard to handle your game, browser, OBS, and other streaming tools. When Stream Together joins the party, it can sometimes be enough to push your system beyond its comfort zone. While Stream Together isn’t the sole cause of these issues, it can be the “final straw” for your system. The good news? Many of these issues can be improved with the right adjustments, which we’ll cover in the following sections.

Step-by-Step Troubleshooting

1. Initial Checks
  • Ensure your OBS and browsers are updated
  • Check your internet connection speed and close any unnecessary browser tabs
  • You can use sites like speedtest.net or fast.com to measure the upload and download speed of your internet connection
2. OBS Optimization
Use Group Browser Source in OBS
  • In Stream Together, click on the top right button labeled ‘Copy Browser Source URL’. You can also access this link in Settings → Browser Sources → Group Automatic Layout
  • Use this single link for your Browser Source in OBS - you can adjust the group layout as needed in Stream Together to format your guests around the screen
Browser Source Settings
  • Right click on your Browser Source in OBS and click ‘Properties’. Then check the “Shutdown source when not visible” option
3. Stream Together Settings

Stream Together has built-in performance settings to help manage system strain. You can locate these settings by clicking the Settings icon at the bottom of your screen and navigating to Performance Settings.

Automatic Optimization
  • If you want Stream Together to manage your settings automatically, enable the setting at the bottom of the page labeled ‘Automatically Optimize my Settings’
Manual Optimization

If you want direct control or your system is still struggling, do the following:

  • Turn off “Automatically Optimize my Settings”
  • Enable “Always Hide Video Preview” - this will turn off video previews of others in backstage and reduce strain (don’t worry, they will still be seen in OBS)
  • Lower the “Maximum Video Quality” setting - this affects the quality of video you send to other call participants and reduces strain

Performance Monitoring Tools for Additional Diagnosis

How to Monitor CPU and Memory Usage

You can monitor CPU and Memory usage on a PC through your Task Manager application, which can be found by clicking your Windows button and searching for “Task Manager”.

Using Task Manager
  • Check the main tab to see all your currently running applications, including your streaming software and any games you have open
  • You can manually end any unneeded programs that are consuming too many resources by selecting the line item and clicking ‘End Task’
  • To check overall CPU and Memory usage click the “Performance Tab”. This tab will show you the maximum capacity of your hardware and the current usage. Use this information to help inform any hardware upgrades

Still Having Issues?

Report Issues

You can report issues directly to our team by clicking the Help icon in the top right corner of Stream Together. Please add as much detail as possible to better help our team understand the issue.

Additional Resources

For more Stream Together guides and information, check out:

  • Getting Started With Stream Together
  • Stream Together Host Guide
  • Stream Together Guest Guide
  • Stream Together FAQs

Need More Help? If you continue experiencing issues after trying these troubleshooting steps, contact Twitch Support with details about your system specifications and the specific problems you’re encountering.

Supported Browsers

The desktop web browser experience of twitch.tv and supporting sites officially support:

  • The two latest versions of Google Chrome
  • The two latest versions of Mozilla Firefox
  • The most recent version of Microsoft Edge
  • The most recent version of Apple Safari
  • The most recent version of Opera and Opera GX

Troubleshooting

While other browsers may work, we cannot guarantee that all features and functionality will operate correctly.

Issues with Non-Supported Browsers

If you are experiencing an issue on a non-supported browser, please contact the appropriate browser’s support team for additional assistance, or please try again on one of our supported browsers.

Issues with Supported Browsers

If you are experiencing an issue on a supported browser, follow these troubleshooting steps in order:

  • Ensure your browser version is up to date.
  • Disable any extensions. Particularly developer extensions, or similar types of extensions.
  • Clear your cache and cookies.
  • It’s important to do this after disabling extensions.
  • Restart your browser and try again.
  • If other steps fail to resolve the issue, log out of VPNs or any other software which might reroute some or all of your requests through a different IP address than your own. This will vary depending on VPN software.
  • Try a different network (e.g., switch from Wi-Fi to mobile data, or try a different Wi-Fi network).
  • Try a different device to determine if the issue is device-specific.

For video or audio playback issues specifically, visit our dedicated Playback Issue Troubleshooting guide.

Contacting Support

If the problem persists after trying the steps above, contact Twitch Support with the following information:

  • Your browser name and version
  • Your operating system
  • Detailed steps to reproduce the issue
  • Screenshots showing the issue
  • Browser console error logs (see instructions below)
How to Collect Browser Error Logs

On Google Chrome:

  • Open your developer console in Chrome. You can do this one of three ways:
    • Right-click your mouse. Choose Inspect
    • Press F12,
    • In the upper right-hand of your browser, select 3 Vertical Dots icon > More tools > Developer Tools,
    • or Press Ctrl + Shift + I
  • Navigate to the Console and Network tabs of your tools.
  • In each window, refresh the page you are having issues with (press F5).
  • Let each page load
  • Screenshot any errors in red
  • Send error log screenshots to support.

On Mozilla Firefox:

  • Open your developer console in Firefox. You can do this one of three ways:
    • Right-click your mouse. Choose Inspect
    • Press F12,
    • Go to Hamburger menu icon (or Tools) > Web Developer > Toggle Tools,
    • or Press Ctrl + Shift + I
  • Navigate to the Network tab of your tools.
  • In that window, load the page you are having issues with (press F5).
  • Let the page load, then sort by Status.
  • Screenshot any errors in red
  • Send error log screenshots to support

Twitch Chat Badges Guide

Chat badges allow you to showcase a part of your identity in channels on Twitch.

There are different types of user badges found on Twitch. To avoid confusion, here is a list of the major chat badge types, ranging from users to staff. No other user type badges are officially sanctioned by Twitch.

On this page:

  • User-Type Chat Badges
  • Chat Badges

User-Type Chat Badges

Twitch Staff:

These are the fine folk who make Twitch tick. Say hello! Twitch Staff badges are reserved for Twitch employees and cannot be granted to community members. Interested in joining the team? Learn more.

Broadcasters:

This is the owner of the Channel that you are currently visiting on Twitch. Broadcasters have the ability to enforce chat rules for their Channel and appoint/remove Channel Moderators.

Chat Moderator:

A member with this icon is a Moderator of the Channel you are currently visiting. They are selected by the Channel owner and have the ability to time out, ban, and enable slow or Subscriber-only mode in this chat.

Lead Moderator:

A member with this icon is a Lead Moderator of the Channel you are currently visiting. Lead moderators have all the abilities of regular moderators, plus additional permissions including managing the mod team, adding/removing VIPs, and accessing all channel moderation settings. Lead moderators can choose to display either the lead mod badge or the regular mod badge.

Partner:

A member with this icon is a Twitch Partner. The Partner Badge uses the same global badge slot shared by Prime, Turbo, Bits, or other badges received from a Twitch Crate opening, not the slot that occupies Broadcaster, Mod, or the others above. All Partners will be automatically granted access to this badge.

Ambassador:

A user with this icon is a member of the Twitch Ambassador Program.

DJ:

A user with this icon is a member of the Twitch DJ program.

VIP:

These are users recognized by streamers as loyal members of their community. VIPs are immune to chat and channel moderation settings, although they are still able to be moderated directly by a channel moderator.

Chat Bot:

Identifies messages from an approved chat bot in a channel. Learn more.

Artist:

Artists are members of a streamer’s community who are recognized for their contributions to the brand/style of the streamer’s channel, such as emotes, overlays, avatars and more. For more information check out our Artist Badge and Attribution article.

Watching without Video:

Anyone who wants to indicate that they are participating in streams without video can use this badge.

Watching without Audio:

Anyone who wants to indicate that they are watching streams with limited or no audio can use this badge.

Some badges are available for a limited time through events or community programs. See our How to Use Badges guide for current and past event badges.

Chat Badges

These are badges available via purchasing subscriptions to various programs on Twitch.

Turbo User:

A subscriber of Twitch’s monthly premium user service. More information can be found here.

Prime User:

A Subscriber of Twitch’s premium user service with additional benefits. More information can be found here.

There are also Cheering Chat Badges and Sub Gifter Badges. Cheering and purchasing Sub Gifts show your support for streamers as well. As you cheer or buy more sub gifts, you earn channel chat badges for that channel so your support is recognized.

Your Cheer Chat Badge lasts indefinitely, but only appears in the channel where you earned it. Your Sub Gift badge lasts until your Sub Gift expires, but your badge levels up permanently in the channel where you earned it.

Show off your support with new Sub Gifter badges between 100-1000… and beyond.

If the channel you’re watching has Leaderboards enabled, you can also earn Top Cheerer, Top Clipper, and Top Gifter badges

You will also find various versions of Subscriber Loyalty Badges based on how long users have been subscribed.

Social Media Badges are earned from helping clips of your favorite streamers go viral. Learn more.

Twitch on TV

On a TV? Chatting, subscribing, and getting help happen on your phone. Scan the QR code on your TV screen to continue there.

You can watch Twitch on your TV with the Twitch app for many smart TVs, streaming devices, and game consoles, or by casting from your phone. Twitch isn’t a TV channel, so you won’t find it in a cable or satellite lineup, and you can’t tune in to it like a broadcast network. What you can do in the app depends on your device. See What You Can Do on Each Device.

Every TV app lets you watch live streams and videos, and browse and search, without signing in. Sign in to see the channels you follow and to follow new ones.

TV apps are built for watching, so anything that takes typing happens on your phone or computer instead. To get started, create your account on twitch.tv, then sign in on your TV. You can read chat on your TV, but to send a message, scan the QR code on your screen and keep chatting on your phone.

Some streams come in both horizontal and vertical versions (Dual Format). TVs are wide screens, so TV apps play the horizontal version. Streams that are only vertical play as usual.

Device Notes

Samsung Smart TVs

You need a Samsung account to install Twitch from the Samsung app store.

To subscribe or gift a sub, go to a channel and select Subscribe (or Gift a Sub if you’re already subscribed). Scan the QR code with your phone and finish on the channel’s subscription page. Sign in with the same Twitch account you use on your TV. To manage your subscriptions, use Twitch on your computer, phone browser, or the Twitch mobile app.

PlayStation and Xbox

The Twitch app on your console is for watching. To go live from your console, use your console’s built-in broadcasting. See PlayStation Broadcasting or Xbox Broadcasting. For problems broadcasting from a PlayStation, contact PlayStation Support.

Casting From Your Phone

You can cast Twitch to a TV with Chromecast from the Twitch mobile app or Chrome.

Sign In

To sign in, choose Log In in the TV app and follow the steps on your screen to finish signing in on your phone or computer. Because you finish there, you can use the same sign-in method you use on your phone, including Google, Apple, or Amazon.

Forgot your password? Reset it on twitch.tv from your phone or computer, then sign in on your TV again.

Get Help

Video won’t play or keeps buffering? Check your internet connection, update the Twitch app and your device’s software, then restart the app. If your app has Report Playback Issues in the video player settings, use it to tell us what happened. Steps to reproduce the problem help most.

2K streams: On devices that can’t play 2K, including LG TVs, the stream plays in 1080p or lower. See 2K Streaming on Twitch.

To report a bug or get help with anything else, contact Twitch Support.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Twitch available on cable or satellite TV?
No. Twitch isn’t a TV channel, so you can’t find it in a cable or satellite lineup. To watch on your TV, use the Twitch app for your smart TV, streaming device, or game console, or cast from your phone. See What You Can Do on Each Device.
Do I need a Twitch account to watch on my TV?
No. You can watch live streams and videos without signing in. Sign in to follow channels.
Can I create a Twitch account on my TV?
No. Create an account on twitch.tv from your phone or computer, then sign in on your TV.
Can I subscribe on my TV?
On Samsung smart TVs, you can subscribe or gift a sub by scanning a QR code with your phone. See Samsung Smart TVs. On other TV apps, subscribe on twitch.tv or in the Twitch mobile app.
Can I stream from my TV?
No. TV apps are for watching. You can go live from a PlayStation or Xbox with your console’s built-in broadcasting. See PlayStation and Xbox.

TwitchRPG Member Info

If you’re already a TwitchRPG member, and need support with receiving Bits or have other survey questions, email the TwitchRPG team at support@rpg.twitch.tv

TwitchRPG (Twitch Research Power Group) is a collaborative community of Twitch viewers, helping provide useful insights and feedback to make Twitch a better place. Simply take surveys and check out the member hub for interesting insights shared out monthly.

TwitchRPG FAQ

Why should I join?
When you join TwitchRPG, your feedback will directly help make Twitch a better place for viewers, creators, and brand partners. Not to mention, some surveys reward Bits, which you can use to support broadcasters.
How do I join?
Visit this link to join! Warning, there are a limited number of seats within the community, so act quickly. If the community is full, don’t worry. We open seats monthly, so check back in!
Can anyone join?
Yes, anyone from anywhere can participate in global surveys! Additionally in 2022, TwitchRPG is expanding into more languages and countries!
How much does membership cost?
TwitchRPG is free to join. We only ask that you keep active, have an opinion, and watch Twitch.
How do I cancel my membership with RPG?
We’d be sad to see you go, but you can remove yourself from RPG by either of the following methods:
  • Opting out through the member portal via the user Information Page. Click ‘Unsubscribe’
  • Request to be removed by emailing support@rpg.twitch.tv
When can I expect a survey?
There are surveys launched daily in several regions around the world. While you will not qualify for all of them, watch Twitch for higher odds.
How often can I take surveys?
Generally, a community member cannot complete more than one survey every two weeks. There are exceptions like administrative or community highlight surveys.
How long do surveys take to finish?
It depends on the study; however, most surveys take between 5-15 minutes.
Where can I give feedback about a survey?
If you have feedback related to the survey’s design, or the content within a survey, please send it here.
How will Twitch use the information I provide?

Depending on the study, your responses will help us understand product features, gaming integrations, advertisement / sponsorship performance, or what we should do next. The majority of information collected is to inform our brand partners on their recent advertising campaigns.

Any information you provide will be used only in accordance with the Twitch Privacy Policy.

What is a sponsored survey?

Twitch partners with a number of brands to help support our creators. Every ad or sponsored broadcast a viewer sees directly impacts a broadcaster’s income. In exchange, Twitch asks RPG members for their feedback on these partnerships or general opinions on a specific industry.

What will I get for completing a sponsored survey?
For every sponsored survey you complete, you’ll receive anywhere between 100 - 500 Bits to use across Twitch on channels that have cheering enabled. Make sure your Twitch ID is confirmed on TwitchRPG to ensure that you receive your Bits.
Does this mean every survey is eligible for Bits rewards?
No, some surveys are for administrative purposes or to engage with the community on hot topics.
How will I know the difference between sponsored surveys and standard ones?
Sponsored surveys will be clearly named “Sponsored Bit Survey”. Also, the email and survey introduction will include language around bit rewards.
How can I be eligible to participate in sponsored surveys?
Everyone is opted in! The more Twitch you watch the more likely you will see more Sponsored Surveys!
How will Bits be delivered?
Bits are paid to the Twitch account linked to your TwitchRPG profile. Bit payment is up to 45 days from completion.
It says my sponsored survey is full, what do I do?
Sponsored surveys are first come first served. If you miss one, don’t worry you’ll still qualify for one in the near future.
It says I don’t qualify for a sponsored survey, what do I do?
Some sponsored surveys require you to have specific experience with a product or service, if you don’t qualify, don’t worry! This does not disqualify you from future surveys.

Understanding Status Updates FAQ

This article is part of a series on giving feedback about Twitch.

The Twitch feedback forums are the place to support ideas that will make Twitch a better place. You can vote or comment on other ideas, or even submit your own.

If you’ve recently posted (or supported) an idea, you may be wondering, “Now what?” This guide walks you through how to give good feedback, and what to expect after publishing your idea.

Public Statuses

Twitch Staff review all submitted ideas and periodically provide updates through a variety of public statuses to summarize which stage of iteration an idea may be in. The table below provides a breakdown of what each status means.

Prior to August 2023, by default, there was no clear way to determine whether an idea has been reviewed by Twitch Staff. Moving forward, we have added a new status Gathering Interest to let you know we’ve read your suggestion and that it’s open for other users to check out.

Public Status

Description

Gathering Interest

An Admin has reviewed this feedback; votes and comments are open for other users to express their support. This is a good time to share your idea with your community!

More Info Needed

There are some questions we need you to answer before we can begin to address this feedback any further.

Investigating

We are determining whether it’d be possible to implement this feedback; this can take any amount of time. This status is also used to let you know we’re investigating the reported bug.

Planned

This idea is on our roadmap.

Looking for Feedback

We are actively looking for feedback on this topic.

Deferred

We are interested in this idea, but it might take a significant amount of time until we might be able to get around to addressing it.

Relevant Update

We have some relevant information for you on this topic. For example, this status can be applied when a feature launches which addresses the feedback provided in some form, although not completely.

Completed

This feedback has been implemented!

Declined

This does not mean the feedback was bad, but we are unable to fulfill it in the foreseeable future.

Comments Closed

This feedback is gathering interest, but the comments are largely off-topic / disparaging to certain individuals or groups (provoking offense).

Closed

The content of the idea is not feedback-related or lacks actionable feedback. Alternatively, we are no longer looking for additional input on an idea previously marked as Looking for Feedback. Learn more about other reasons an idea might have been closed.

When possible, we will try to provide context to the public status provided. When other members vote/comment on your idea, or when Twitch has an update for you, you’ll receive an email from Twitch to the address you verified in account settings. Please remember, we can’t address or act on every piece of feedback we receive.

Product development is complex - plans might change. There is no single linear path in statuses for an idea to follow.

Responding to Status Updates

Sometimes, we might reach out to clarify with a status (especially for status More Info Needed). To respond, please use the thumbs up/down buttons in the email you receive (titled: Twitch has updated the status of an idea you support!), to be taken to a web form. Ensure you hit Submit Feedback.

Please note that if you try to respond by clicking on the idea title and leaving a comment, we won’t be able to know. Using the method described ensures we are notified of your response.

Managing Notifications

If you have an idea with a lot of activity and find yourself overwhelmed by new comments, you can manage your notifications.

Go to the Settings found under your username in the top, right corner of the page to turn off notifications for New comments. We do not recommend turning off notifications for status updates – these emails will help you stay in the know regarding any developments with the ideas you have posted or supported.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was my idea closed?

In general, it’s hard to implement every idea, so we’re counting a lot on the votes given by our users to see which features they need the most. If an idea is not gaining much traction and showing low activity, it will eventually be closed to clear up space for other ideas that can be discovered. You can always resubmit an idea.

An idea might also be closed, because it is not feedback-related (appeals or commentary on suspension decisions, support requests, suggestions disparaging others), lacks actionable feedback (offers little to no insight/is non-constructive), or falls into a category that is unsupported.

Ideas with feedback on multiple topics are generally closed, as it is hard to determine which portion of the idea users might be agreeing with when supporting it with a vote. In this case, we will prompt you to post the various pieces of feedback separately.

Be sure to check out these tips on how to provide actionable feedback.

Why was my idea archived?

Ideas posted in regard to a feature/function that has been deprecated are not supported, so they may be moved to a private forum called Archived.

Archived feedback is not accessible to the community.

You may also see your idea in Archived, as we periodically clean the forums in terms of ideas that Closed to make it easier for users to review them. Unless products are deprecated, most ideas that are archived are those that have remained relatively inactive in terms of votes & comments. Please feel free to repost your ideas and give it a new shot for support, provided it doesn’t revolve around a deprecated feature/function.

A suggestion I created or supported has a lot of upvotes, but no reply - why?

Votes on a suggestion give us general, quantifiable data regarding how many people are genuinely interested in the idea, which is incredibly useful when making decisions or taking feedback into consideration.

Our goal is to reply to as many ideas as we can and provide as much information in regard to them as possible; however, sometimes, we just aren’t ready to share, or need to have additional discussions internally first.

It’s important to note that just because an idea has a high vote count, doesn’t mean it will automatically get accepted. Nonetheless, when having our internal conversations, it is very important for us to gauge user interest.

I am seeing a message that my idea was merged – what does this mean?

We merge similar ideas to keep our feedback forums organized, easy to search, and to ensure that all votes (interest) are consolidated as best as possible. When an idea is merged:

  • All unique votes, plus its comments will be combined into the idea that it was merged into.
  • The description of the idea will show as a comment in the idea it was merged into.
  • Clicking on the URL of the merged idea will show users a message that explains the idea has been merged and includes a link that redirects them to the idea it was merged into.

Please keep this in mind when trying to create the same idea in various categories or quantities.

While our goal is to merge any new ideas into the oldest similar idea, there are instances in which we merge older ideas into newer ones, provided they have a clearer title and/or description.

Why Can’t I Chat?

If you’re having trouble sending chat messages on Twitch, there are several common reasons this might happen. This guide will help you identify and resolve the issue.

This guide is for troubleshooting chat messages in channels. If you’re having trouble sending Whispers (direct messages), visit our Whispers guide.

Quick Check

Before troubleshooting, ask yourself these questions:

  • Does this happen in more than one channel?
  • Do I have a stable internet connection?
  • Am I seeing any error messages or prompts in chat?

If the issue only happens in one channel, it’s likely related to that channel’s specific settings or restrictions. If it happens across multiple channels, continue reading below.

Common Reasons

Here are the most common reasons your chat messages might not be going through:

Connection Issues

An unstable or weak internet connection is the most common reason for chat problems. If your connection drops or is slow, your messages may not send. Try:

  • Checking your internet connection strength
  • Refreshing the page or restarting the Twitch app
  • Switching to a more stable network if possible
Email or Phone Verification Required

Many channels require chatters to verify their email address or phone number before sending messages. If you see a prompt asking you to verify, you’ll need to complete verification to chat in that channel.

  • Verify your email address
  • Learn more about phone verification
  • Learn about Chat Verification Settings

If you’re having trouble verifying your email or phone number, contact Twitch Support for help.

You’ve Been Banned from the Channel

If you’ve been banned from a specific channel’s chat, you won’t be able to send messages there. Channel bans are set by the channel owner or their moderators and only affect that specific channel.

If the channel owner has enabled Unban Requests, you may be able to request to be unbanned. Learn more about bans and Unban Requests.

You’ve Been Blocked

If someone has blocked you, you won’t see their messages and they won’t see yours. Blocking works in both directions, meaning, you won’t be notified if someone blocks you. Learn more about blocking.

Your Account Has Received a Chatting Suspension

If your account has been suspended by Twitch for violating our Terms of Service or Community Guidelines, you cannot chat in any channel until the suspension is lifted.

Check your account status and appeal suspensions at appeals.twitch.tv. Learn more about account suspensions.

Can’t Send GIF Messages?

If you’re specifically having trouble sending GIFs in chat, it may be for one of these reasons:

  • You are not subscribed at Tier 2 or higher in this channel
  • The streamer has disabled GIF keyboard for their channel
  • The channel is in Emote-Only Mode, Shield Mode, or another mode that prevents GIF messages
  • The streamer does not have access to GIF keyboard

Learn more about GIF Keyboard on Twitch.

Still Having Trouble?

If none of the above reasons apply to your situation, there are a few other possibilities:

  • New account: Very new accounts may experience temporary limitations as part of our efforts to prevent abuse. Continue using your account normally and this should resolve on its own.
  • Automated protection: In rare cases, your account’s chat connection may be temporarily restricted due to automated safety measures. This can happen if we detect unusual patterns of activity.

If you’ve checked all the common reasons above and are still unable to chat, contact Twitch Support for further assistance.

Frequently Asked Questions

I can chat in some channels but not others. Why?
Different channels have different requirements for chatting. Some channels require email or phone verification, while others may have follower-only mode or other restrictions enabled. Check if you’re seeing any prompts in the chat window asking you to verify your account or meet other requirements.
How do I know if I’ve been banned from a channel?
If you’ve been banned from a channel, you’ll typically see a message in the chat window indicating that you cannot send messages. The message may also tell you if the ban is temporary (a timeout) or permanent.
What’s the difference between being banned and being suspended?
A ban is channel-specific and prevents you from chatting in one particular channel. A suspension is a site-wide enforcement action by Twitch that restricts your entire account. Learn more about bans, blocking, and suspensions.
I verified my email or phone number, but still can’t chat. What should I do?
After verifying your email or phone number, try refreshing the page or restarting the app. Some channels may also have additional requirements like follower-only mode, or slow mode. If you’re still having trouble, contact Twitch Support for help.
Can I chat if my account is very new?
Yes, but some channels have settings that require accounts to exist for a certain period of time before you can chat. Additionally, very new accounts may occasionally experience temporary limitations as part of our automated safety measures. These typically resolve as you continue using your account normally.

Getting Started: Beginner Broadcasting

About Virtual Cameras

An introduction into virtual cameras, how to use them, and helpful tips on using them in Stream Together as well as other streaming tools.

What are Virtual Cameras?

Virtual cameras are software tools that allow the same video source to be utilized in multiple applications, to be used so you can share your screen, specific streaming software scenes, and cameras. Virtual cameras act as a camera source, and various software tools provide them. Because of this, the core application for the virtual camera needs to be running while the virtual camera is in use.

Who needs Virtual Cameras?

There are multiple uses for virtual cameras, however the primary users are those using Windows on PC. Windows has device exclusivity, meaning that once a device is being utilized by one application it cannot be used by a second. For streamers, this means that if you are using your camera in your streaming software, you cannot use it in another application like Stream Together, Zoom, Discord, etc. at the same time.

For many streamers, this means that if you are using your camera in your streaming software, you cannot use it in another application like Stream Together, Zoom, Discord, etc. at the same time. at the same time without using a virtual camera.

Virtual cameras duplicate a camera you already use, so you can use it in other applications.

How to Set Up a Virtual Camera in OBS

OBS Version 28.0 and Above

Follow the below instructions to use an OBS virtual camera in version 28.0 and above

  • Open yours OBS
  • Click Start Virtual Camera button in main OBS control area
  • Select Virtual Camera Settings
  • Select Source under Output Type
  • Select your desired Video Capture Device under Output Selection
  • In Stream Together/other application, you can now select the virtual camera as a device
Below OBS Version 28.0

Follow the below instructions to use an OBS virtual camera in a pre V28.0 build of OBS

  • Download the OBS Virtual Cam plugin here: obsproject.com
  • Proceed through the install wizard
  • Close OBS and restart your PC
  • Open OBS
  • Right click on your video capture device source of the camera you want to use, then click Filter
  • Add an Effect Filter and choose Virtual Cam
  • Click Start
  • Click Close
  • In Stream Together/other application, you can now select this virtual camera as a device

How to Set Up A Virtual Camera in Streamlabs

We recommend using OBS for virtual cameras, as their virtual cameras are built out and more functional than in Streamlabs. Streamlabs has marked their virtual camera as experimental. To use a Streamlabs virtual camera, follow the below instructions:

  • Go to Settings, then Virtual Webcam
  • CLick Install Virtual Webcam
  • Click Start Virtual Webcam
  • The virtual camera will capture the active scene in Streamlabs, and that will be what the output of the virtual camera. Because of this, your virtual camera output will be of what you are streaming, not just your traditional camera (face cam, vtuber model, etc)
  • In Stream Together/other application, you can now select this virtual camera as a device

Uses of Virtual Cameras

You can use virtual cameras to capture webcams, active stream scenes, entire applications, and more. Below are some examples of how to use a virtual camera to get your gears turning!

  • Show your face-cam in Stream Together so you can stream with friends, all showing the same face cams while playing a game together, chatting about your favorite topics, or reacting to content
  • Show your gameplay in Stream Together, by pointing your virtual camera at your game application/scene you can show your gameplay to your friends in Stream Together and they can show it on their stream in a browser source
  • Show your stream scenes in Zoom, Discord, etc, by pointing your virtual camera at your scene, you can show your stream in online calls; this doesn’t just have to be gaming, this can be helpful for demonstrations and presentations as well.

Adding Tags to A Stream

Like a stream title, tags should be changed each time you go live. Tags set the context of your stream and let others discover you more easily.

Tags are highly visible to viewers, and are shown alongside the video thumbnail, stream title, and the game or category anytime you see a video on Twitch. If a viewer finds your stream from one of your custom tags, you can review this information in your Discovery Analytics. Learn more.

On this page:

  • What Type of Tags Should I Add?
  • Adding Tags in Stream Manager
  • Safety & Moderation
  • Frequently Asked Questions

What Type of Tags Should I Add?

Channel owners and editors can add any tag to your stream that they like, provided that it meets our moderation criteria and the community guidelines. Add tags to a stream that capture your personality, the type of content you are making, or your country affiliation.

For example: A Music streamer who primarily sings requested songs might tag their stream with requests. Viewers searching for requests can find their content. Viewers browsing can know what to expect with this stream.

You don’t need to add the name of the game or category you are streaming in, as this is automatically applied.

Adding Tags in Stream Manager

Some tags are automatically applied by the Category you are streaming to.

On twitch.tv, navigate to your Creator Dashboard -> Stream Manager -> Edit Stream Info. Add up to 10 custom tags to describe yourself or the content of your upcoming stream.

On the Twitch mobile app, enter Creator Mode. Select Edit Stream Info and add up to 10 custom tags to describe yourself or the content of your upcoming stream.

Adding Tags in Third-Party Apps

Tags can be set in some third-party broadcasting software.

(Visit Streamlabs for support)

Channel owners using third-party broadcasting software that does not support tags can add tags to their stream in the Edit Stream Info Quick Action in your Stream Manager.

At this time, custom tags cannot be added when going live on consoles like Xbox or PlayStation devices.

Safety & Moderation

Channel owners and editors can add any tag to your stream that they like, provided that it meets our moderation criteria and the community guidelines.

All tags go through a multi-layer moderation process including proactive detection to prevent improper language from being used. We also will be regularly updating a prohibited tag list, which will remove tags from circulation. Twitch accounts can be reported for using abusive or harmful tags that violate Twitch’s Community Guidelines.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are tags case sensitive?
No! For example, all streams tagged with “Cat”, “cat”, “cAt”, “caT”, or “CAT” can be found at twitch.tv/directory/all/tags/cat
How do tags function across multiple languages?
Tags are not automatically translated and do not connect the same word across different languages. So, streams tagged with “gato,” “mačka”, “кіт”, “kot”, or “แมว” will be found in separate tag directories. However, multiple tags using the same alphabet, characters, or accents will compile together, similar to hashtags and tagging systems you’d find on other platforms.

Check out this help article for more information about the languages on Twitch.

Does Twitch provide discovery metrics for tags?
Yes! Visit your channel insights, and review ‘What tags are users filtering by to find my channel?’ There needs to be enough data for this panel to show you results. Learn more about channel insights.
Can tags have spaces?
No.
Can one tag contain more than one word?
Yes. For alphabetic languages, you can delineate between the words with capital letters (e.g. IndieGame) if you would like to delineate multiple words in a single tag.
Are tags alphanumeric?
We allow letters, numbers, and many accent marks. Special characters are not allowed.
Is there a limit to the number of tags I can add to my stream?
You can use up to 10 tags. We may increase this limit in the future.
Is there a limit to the number of characters I can add to my tags?
Yes, there’s a limitation of 25 maximum characters per tag.
How is the language tag set on my stream?
Some tags are applied automatically, including the language of your stream. Language tag is selected by your chosen site language.

Learn more in our knowledge guide: help.twitch.tv/s/article/languages-on-twitch

Can I add tags for other attributes?
Yes, of course. Streamers can use tags for any topic they would like to organize around as long as it does not violate our Community Guidelines.

Broadcasting Guidelines

See Twitch Ingest Recommendations for ingest server recommendations.

Our guidelines are set up in a way to find the right balance between visual quality and playback quality, where both the broadcaster and the viewer can benefit from. Read the info below to help you choose the Encoding, Bitrate, Resolution, and Framerate settings that provide the right balance for the game you’re playing, your internet speed, and your computer’s hardware. Remember: it’s always better to have a stable stream than to push for a higher video quality that might cause you to drop frames or test the limits of your internet connection.

Encoding

Encoding Performance

Encoding can be taxing on your system. x264 will utilize a lot of your CPU, resulting in lower FPS. Alternatively, GPU encoding (e.g. NVIDIA NVENC) utilizes a dedicated encoder in the GPU, allowing you to play and stream without compromising game performance. If you want to use x264, start with veryfast preset, and experiment with them until you find your sweet spot.

Encoding Quality

x264 offers a wide range of presets that change quality significantly, and presets above Faster require CPUs with 6+ cores. NVIDIA NVENC offers consistent quality based on the generation of the encoder. The updated NVIDIA Encoder (NVENC) on Turing-based NVIDIA GeForce GPUs (RTX 20-Series and GTX 1660/Ti) will typically produce superior quality than x264 Fast and on par with x264 medium. While the older generation (Pascal, Kepler) are similar with veryfast/faster quality.

Internet Speed (bitrate)

Your ingest bitrate is the amount of data you send to Twitch when you stream. A higher bitrate takes up more of your available internet bandwidth. Increasing your bitrate can improve your video quality, but only up to a certain point– our recommended bitrate settings have been tested to optimize video quality without wasting bandwidth.

CBR vs VBR

You may have noticed the option to select between VBR (variable bitrate) and CBR (constant bitrate). Twitch suggests that all Broadcasters use CBR for several reasons, all of which relate to the final quality of service (QoS) that your viewers will experience.

The main problem with VBR is that during lulls in the action: paused games, hero selection screens, etc, VBR streams produce a significantly lower bitrate. This can cause issues (stream buffering, dropped frames) with many end-user connections when the bitrate spikes back up during the action (team fights, high motion scenes).

VBR also leads to issues when sending data to the Twitch network over many ISPs. When connecting to Twitch, the route your ISP takes may not be stable enough to handle sudden increases in bandwidth, leading to “broadcast starvation.”

Broadcast starvation (instability) is when video data does not arrive in a timely fashion or is completely missing. This happens when there are network problems between you and Twitch, when you attempt to stream at a bitrate that is too high for your network/ISP, or have problems with your router causing frames to be dropped before entering the Twitch network. This leads to lag for everyone (including people watching on your lower resolutions), buffering, and stream disconnections.

Variable bitrate is suboptimal for video over the internet due to how TCP (the internet protocol most streaming video uses) works, and you should use CBR whenever possible.

Video Quality

Resolution refers to the size of a video on a screen, and frame rate refers to how often animation frames are sent to Twitch. Full HD resolution is typically 1080p, 60 frames per second (fps). Streaming at a higher resolution like 1080p requires a higher bitrate, and a higher frame rate takes more encoding power. If you have the bandwidth and encoding power to stream at 1080p, 60 fps, great! If not, try one of the recommended settings below to optimize your video quality and stability.

Audio Quality

Twitch iOS app streamers, check your broadcast setup against Apple’s recommendations here: developer.apple.com/documentation

  • Codec: AAC-LC. Stereo or Mono
  • Recommended Bitrate (for maximum compatibility) 96kbps
  • Maximum audio bit rate: 160 kbps (AAC)
  • Sampling frequency: any (AAC)

Other Useful Info

The maximum broadcast length is 48 hours. This cannot be changed. Reconnection behavior may depend on encoder used.
