Getting Started with Stream Together

Stream Together is currently in Beta – this means some planned features are still a work-in-progress. An earlier version of this product was named “Guest Star.”

Stream Together helps streamers collaborate on-stream with other streamers across multiple live channels, or as guests on a single channel. Stream Together makes it easy for streamers to bring members of their community live on stream.

Collaborating is a fun way to reach new audiences and grow. Stream Together is built to maximize ways viewers can discover and follow you when you’re live with others.

Current requirements for Stream Together:

  • You need to stream from a desktop computer
  • Your Twitch account must be Phone Verified
  • You’ll need to link your Streaming Software (OBS, Streamlabs, etc) to a Stream Together session, which you’ll manage in a Google Chrome web browser*

*Other browsers will be supported in the future, during the beta phase, Chrome is recommended.

If you experience OBS crashes, laggy video feeds, audio problems, or high CPU usage while using Stream Together, check our Stream Together Troubleshooting Guide for step-by-step optimization solutions.

Here’s a step-by-step guide for how to get started.

Step 1: Open Stream Together & Configure Your Webcam & Microphone

If you’ve been invited as a guest for a Stream Together session and need help with setup, refer to our guide: Joining as a Stream Together Guest

From your Creator Dashboard, open Stream Together This will start a Stream Together session.

You can set up Stream Together as a Quick Action shortcut in your Stream Manager

Look for the camera and microphone icons at the bottom of the session, and use them to configure your own video and audio settings.

If your Twitch account isn’t phone verified, you will receive a prompt to verify it via phone. You will not be able to proceed with Stream Together until your Twitch account has been phone verified.

For Windows Users - OBS Virtual Camera Quick Setup

This product works with any broadcasting software that supports browser sources; however, we recommend using it with OBS. If you choose to use another broadcasting software and a single webcam, it may require additional setup to install and use a virtual camera in that software.

Windows users may find their webcam used in OBS is not available in Stream Together. This is because Windows allows webcam use in only one program at a time. To resolve this issue, we recommend you use the OBS Virtual Camera which duplicates your camera feed into OBS. This will allow your stream to show up as your camera in Stream Together. To do so:

  • Make sure OBS is open.
  • In OBS select Start Virtual Camera
  • Select OBS Virtual Camera in Stream Together

Once set up, your camera in Stream Together will show your stream, allowing you to start inviting guests and collaborating.

Step 2: Connect the Stream Together Feed to Your Streaming Software as a Browser Source

Your Stream Together browser source link is a video feed sent to your streaming software. You can find and manage this link in the “Settings” button located in the top navigation bar or the “Browser Source Settings” button in the right panel.

  • Copy the Group Automatic Layout Link
  • Go to your streaming software and select the scene you want to use for Stream Together
  • Create a new Browser Source and paste the link

With Group Automatic Layout / Output, all guests in the stream are captured in one browser source. This will feel similar to traditional conferencing software like Zoom, or Google Meet.

Advanced: Manage Guest Feeds Through Individual Browser Sources - If you want to customize how individual guest feeds display on your stream, you can set your scene up using individual browser source links.

Advanced Audio Settings

The default audio setting recommended for most users is Desktop Audio Capture. This setting mutes browser sources to prevent doubled audio.

You can adjust for advanced audio setups in the Browser Source Audio settings. If you prefer to control sources in streaming sources, select Control Audio via Streaming software. This means audio will come out of your browser tab as well as your browser sources and you may experience doubled audio if your desktop audio is outputting to your stream. You can control the source’s audio through your streaming software’s audio mixer.

More tips for troubleshooting audio can be found here.

Step 3: Invite Collaborators or Guests

With Stream Together, you guests can stream the session on their own channels, using their own browser source links. As the host of a call, you can disable this option.

To invite a guest, follow these simple steps:

  • Click the “Invite” button located in the right panel.
  • Search for the Twitch channel of the guest you wish to invite.
  • If you don’t want your guests to have the option of streaming the session, you’ll see the option to disable.

Alternatively, you can provide other collaborators with an Invite Link found in the same pop-up window. This link can be regenerated on demand.

Find a step-by-step setup guide for guests here.

After a guest accepts their invitation and prepares their camera and microphone, you can click “Add to Call” button next to that user’s name in the right-hand panel. They’ll be added to the “backstage” of your session.

If your guest mentions they haven’t received an invite notification, you can follow the steps in our troubleshooting tips to whisper a link that will allow your guest to join.

Step 4: Push your Guests to Your Streaming Software

Once you’ve added your guest, you’ll be able to see and hear them in the “Backstage” area. If you everything seems right, the next step is to send the feed to your streaming software.

To push the guest’s feed to your broadcasting software, follow these steps:

  • Hover your cursor over the slot where the guest is located.
  • Click the “Show on Stream” toggle that appears.
  • If a dialog modal asks you to confirm the action, click “Yes, Push Guest.”

Your guest’s feed should appear in your streaming software scene. You’re now live!

After your guest is pushed to your broadcasting software, you will be able to see them within your scene. If you haven’t started your live stream yet, both you and your guest are now ready to go live on your stream. Issues? Check out these articles:

  • Troubleshooting Audio

Frequently Asked Questions

Guide to Broadcast Health

Did you know? Twitch Inspector is a tool available to all creators that provide critical stream health information in a visible, digestible format. Learn more about Twitch Inspector in our Guide to Broadcast Health and Using Twitch Inspector.

Most stream problems will appear in the Bitrate Graph displayed within a stream in Twitch Inspector. The graph shows bitrates out of the broadcaster’s encoder and how they look once they arrive at our ingest server.

Here are the most common issues and how you can fix them:

How to Check Broadcast Health

When troubleshooting stream problems, it’s essential to understand what elements of the stream pipeline you do and do not have control over. Each layer of the streaming pipeline can introduce more complexity, even before your stream reaches Twitch’s servers. So let’s break it down:

  • Focus first on settings you control within your broadcast software.
  • The pipeline starts with you. When troubleshooting, try adjusting settings like bitrate, framerate, video resolution, and encoder presets according to our broadcast guidelines: These local adjustments often have the most immediate results in improving your stream quality before connecting your device to the internet.
  • Reduce complexity in how your broadcast device connects to a local network by utilizing wired (ethernet) connection over wireless whenever possible. If using Wi-Fi, your signal strength and the number of devices on the same network will influence your ability to broadcast reliably.
  • Next, check how your device is connected to the internet.
  • After you configure your broadcast and network, your stream hits the public internet on its way to the Twitch servers. How your device is connected to this network can introduce issues. Factors like your ISP/public internet, outages, local maintenance, and general internet congestion can impact your stream on its way to the Twitch ingest server. You may have limited control over these factors.
  • Twitch ingest accepts your stream and prepares to beam it to the world.
  • At this point, your stream is broken down from the source quality and transformed and optimized so your viewers can watch it on different devices like TVs, consoles, mobile, their desktops at various qualities. If you experience issues, you can change your Twitch ingest server.

Question on transcodes? Visit Transcodes FAQ

Common Issues

Currently live? Review bitrate settings and other stream health info from your Creator Dashboard.

Local Network Problems

If lowering the bitrate and checking the encoder settings does not eliminate instability, it could be intermittent connectivity issues. The issues could be a broken cable, spotty Wi-Fi, problems in the local internet, or some other processes inadvertently consuming internet bandwidth.

Ensure that no other computers or devices are consuming the internet bandwidth, the modem router is undamaged, and there are no problems in the region.

Dropped Frames

Most broadcast software alerts you if frames from your broadcast are not reaching Twitch servers. If your broadcast software indicates you are dropping frames, try the following:

  • Check your ingest server. Make sure you have the best server selected for your location and network. Visit our recommended ingest endpoints: help.twitch.tv/twitch-ingest-recommendation.
  • Check your upload speed. You may be throttled or have local network issues preventing you from uploading at your current bitrate.
  • If you still have issues, lower your bitrate live – most broadcast software allows you to do this – until frames stop dropping.
  • Streaming at a bitrate close to the limit of your internet connection’s maximum may add delay to your stream. If viewers complain about accumulating delay, and the bitrate graph shows a flat line, the connection may be hitting its limit, even though it seems okay. Lower the bitrate by 200 to 500 kbps; this should vastly improve the connection while having minimal effect on visual quality.
Low Internet Bandwidth

The stream is relatively unstable, even when lowering bitrates. In these cases, there is insufficient bandwidth between the ISP and Twitch, or something needs to be fixed in the network path to Twitch. To resolve this, switch to a different Twitch server, check that no other network process is using bandwidth, or contact your ISP for network diagnostics.

Excessive High Bitrate

Here the broadcaster is streaming at 14,000 kbps. Simply using a higher bitrate does not necessarily mean better quality; in this case, such a high bitrate is causing instability. Remember to adhere to a maximum of 6000. In many cases, high bandwidth causes stream instability throughout a broadcast.

Network or Hardware Problems

Sometimes the machine doing the video encoding has issues keeping up with the load (video encoding takes a lot of computing resources). In this case, verify the device is not overloaded, running too many things at a time, and that the encoder is up to date. Then, switch to an encoding preset that uses less CPU.

Check your router configuration - does it support your internet?

When possible, avoid WiFi as this can create an unstable network environment.

Other common issues could be software, such as anti-virus, proxies, needing to update network cards, OS, GPU, or having too many programs open.

Possible Network Path Errors

If a well-configured stream that used to work fine starts to show instability, it may be a case of network path errors. Try switching Twitch ingest servers (to change the network path from the encoder to Twitch) and lowering bitrate, which can help stability.

Bitrate Spikes

This stream may use a variable bitrate or a streaming encoder that is not correctly limiting the bitrate. While the average bitrate is around 3500 kbps, 4500 kbps spikes will cause viewers to buffer and experience issues. Also, very high bitrate spikes will cause persistent buffering for viewers. To avoid this, specify a constant bitrate or lower the bitrate.

Bitrate Dips

Sometimes streaming encoders try to be too smart and optimize bitrate. If the bitrate dips, when the bitrate goes back up, viewers will experience buffering from trying to load too much data. Try testing with a different encoder. Be aware that dips can also happen if your machine may need more CPU power for the encoder to compress video.

Guide to Using Twitch Inspector

Uh-oh… Chat, can you hear me? Stream tech problems can be frustrating.

The Twitch Inspector tool provides key details about the health and specification of each of your streams to help you analyze the health of your broadcast and troubleshoot any issues that occur.

Compare your stream specs in Twitch Inspector against our suggested guidelines here.

  • Visit Creator Camp for stream setup guides, quick-start walkthroughs, and more!
  • What’s bitrate? Skip to the Inspector glossary to understand key terms.
  • For recommended settings, visit our guidelines here.
  • For troubleshooting tips, visit Guide to Stream Health.

Twitch Inspector At a Glance

Log in to Twitch Inspector at inspector.twitch.tv to review a complete list of your streams in the last 7 days.

You’ll need to authorize Twitch Inspector to access your account.

Use caution to protect the information in Twitch Inspector.

Once you log in, this list from the last 7 days includes all streams, regardless of device (i.e. console, mobile phone, laptop/PC).

  • A. Start Date/Time - When your stream began. The time should be your local timezone. It is in 24-hour format.
  • B. Duration - How long your stream lasted. If your stream starts and stops a lot, you’ll see multiple additions to this list, including bandwidth tests.
  • C. Streaming Tool - This is the tool that you used to stream to Twitch. You can stream to Twitch from a variety of sources.
  • D. Twitch Server - This is where your stream is sent. Most streaming software sets this for you automatically. You can check your local Twitch ingest server at here.
  • E. Unstable Events - Events that are unstable in Twitch. If you have a high number of these events, you could be experiencing issues.

Twitch Inspector Glossary

Within Inspector are a number of streaming video terms. The following glossary should help you interpret the information in Inspector, as well as our recommended settings here.

Learn more about setting up your stream in Creator Camp:

Setting

Description

Bitrate

Your bitrate is the amount of data you send to Twitch when you stream. A higher bitrate takes up more of your available internet bandwidth. Increasing your bitrate can improve your video quality, but only up to a certain point. View our recommended bitrate settings here, which have been tested to optimize video quality without wasting bandwidth.

Stream settings that do not match our recommended settings can cause video playback issues for viewers (such as viewers can hear audio, but experience no video). If you experience fluctuation between Max/Min bitrate, visit our guide to review recommended bitrate settings.

Frame Rate (fps)

Frame rate refers to how often animation frames are sent to Twitch. Full HD resolution is typically 60 frames per second (fps). If you have the bandwidth and encoding power to run 60 fps, great! If not, try adjusting to 30 fps or another of the recommended settings here.

Video Resolution

This is the resolution that your stream is sent to Twitch. You may have your game or other elements of your stream set to other resolutions. The resolution shown here is the final resolution sent to Twitch. While it is possible to stream in other aspect ratios/resolutions, most viewing devices and streaming programs best support an aspect ratio of 16:9.

Configuration Check

This is a check for your configuration. If you’re green, you’re good to go. If your configuration check is red, follow the remediation steps in the error.

Session ID

The unique identifier for your stream. This is not the same as your Stream Key. If you contact Twitch Support and need help, provide this information.

For questions on your stream key, visit the Twitch Stream Key Guide & FAQ.

Audio/Video Codec

Most streaming software will set this for you, however some may allow you to set this yourself. Codecs work to compress and decompress your audio and video for streaming.

AVC Level

AVC (Advanced Video Coding, or H.264 encoding) is an advanced setting within most streaming software.

Keyframe Interval

When adjusted beyond the default, certain viewers on certain devices may have difficulty viewing your stream.

Delay

Twitch is primarily a live service focused on the real-time interactions between audience and streamer. Occasionally, a delay can be added. You can add a delay in most streaming software.

Encoder (Streaming Tool)

This is the streaming software that sends your stream to Twitch.

Twitch Server

A Twitch ingest server is where your stream enters our network from the public internet. We usually automatically select the closest server to your location. Sometimes switching to a new ingest server can help resolve network issues.

RTMP Header

RTMP is the name of the video streaming protocol used by Twitch. The RTMP header contains technical details relevant to your streaming software configuration. Thankfully, the most relevant info within this header is surfaced in other settings, such as bitrate or video resolution.

Broadcast Format

Live or rerun.

Stitch Source

For power users utilizing failover protection or other advanced stream settings.

Stream Health Graphs in Inspector

Twitch Inspector contains a number of helpful health checks in the form of graphs. Learn more in Guide to Stream Health.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who can access Twitch Inspector?
All broadcasters may use Twitch Inspector. Only you, the broadcaster, may access Twitch Inspector for your stream. Moderators and editors cannot access Twitch Inspector for streams other than their own.
Where can I access Twitch Inspector?
Twitch Inspector is available via a web browser only at Inspector.Twitch.Tv. Twitch Inspector is not available via Twitch mobile apps. However, you may access the web page on a mobile web browser.
What is a Twitch ingest server?
When you broadcast to Twitch, you send your stream over the public internet to a Twitch ingest server. At this point, Twitch verifies and prepares your stream to distribute it around the world. Learn more here.
Do I need to choose a Twitch ingest server?
Most software and services choose the best (closest) Twitch ingest server for you. Broadcast streams enter Twitch through an ingest server, where they are authorized and registered, then prepared for viewers. Choosing the ingest server closest to you should result in lowest ping for your viewers. It can be a good idea to test your broadcast every time you move location or change ISP.
  • In XSplit, ping timings are shown automatically in a drop-down box.
  • For OBS and other tools, try this.
  • If in doubt, use the server physically closest to you.

If in doubt, use the server physically closest to you.

If you need to construct an RTMP URL for your chosen Twitch server, please visit our Twitch Stream Key & URL Guide.

What can Twitch Inspector do for me?
Twitch Inspector can aid in troubleshooting past broadcasts.
Can I use Twitch Inspector to run a test stream?
Yes! A key benefit of Twitch Inspector is the ability to run a test stream. You can add the information here to the end of your stream key.

For more information visit Twitch Stream Key FAQ.

How Does Search Work?

This page describes how to use search and answers some frequently asked questions.

What is Search?

Search is one of the primary content discovery features on the Twitch website, iOS and Android apps, mobile web and TV Apps.

The search field is accessible from the magnifying glass in the Twitch mobile app or in the top navigation bar on twitch.tv.

Suggestions

Type any word or phrase to see search suggestions. Search suggestions provide shortcuts to popular channel names or categories.

Results and Ranking

Search works best when searching for the exact channel name, category, tag, or VOD title.

  • Enter any word or phrase
  • Press Enter to see search results

Select Show More to expand the options on mobile and desktop.

Which Channels Appear in Suggestions?

When typing into the search box, we will surface relevant suggestions to aid your search. If your channel does not appear in search suggestions, it could be that your channel is not searched frequently enough yet to show in suggestions. This is not necessarily a bug.

Don’t see your channel in search suggestions? Click enter and check search results!

Which Channels Appear in Search Results

A channel may not show up in search results for any of these 3 reasons:

  • The channel is banned
  • The channel is geoblocking in your region
  • The channel has not streamed once in the last 365 days

Learn more about geoblocking in our knowledge guide: help.twitch.tv/s/article/geoblocking

Frequently Asked Questions

Search logic may change over time without notice. These answers do not represent solely how search logic works, but are meant to generally help you understand common search questions.

How do search suggestions work?

When you type words or phrases in the search input box, we check if those search words or phrases match with a channel name (or its display name), a category name, or other user-entered search queries so that it can prefix suggestions.

Channels, categories and frequently searched queries are ranked using a number of factors. The top results will be shown in search suggestions.

Some example factors are:

  • How frequently a particular query (including channel or category names) were searched
  • How frequently the displayed suggestion was clicked

Channels eligible for suggestions need to have streamed once in the last 365 days, and not currently suspended.

What is the difference between ranking in search suggestions and search results?

Search results are not the same as search suggestions. Suggestions exist to guide a user to select a search term. Suggestions shown are usually prefixed to what the user has typed. Meanwhile, search results take into account a variety of different factors in ranking the results.

What aspects of my channel are used in search results and ranking?

Various factors are used to rank items on the search result page. Some examples include:

  • Channel name or login
  • Category of the stream
  • Tags
  • Stream title
  • Social media username

A live channel I am searching for appears offline in search results. Why?

There can be a delay in updating search with information such as whether a channel is live or offline, which game the channel is streaming, the title of the stream, its tags or other such information.

My channel used to be ranked first in results for a particular query. Why has this changed?

It is expected behavior if your channel ranking changes at different times.

A number of factors can impact where a particular channel ranks in search results. These factors include but are not limited to:

  • how frequently the channel was clicked from search suggestions
  • how frequently the channel was clicked from search results
  • whether or not the channel is live or offline
  • many other factors

I just started my first live stream. How long will it take for me to appear in search results?

Not very long at all. Usually within 10 minutes, but it can take up to 60 minutes.

Once unsuspended, how long does it take for a channel to show up in search results, or search suggestions?

It may take up to 60 minutes for unsuspended channels to show up on search results, and up to 48 hours to show in search suggestions.

Can I search for scheduled streams?

Not directly. If a channel has a scheduled stream and is the top result, the next scheduled stream will appear.

Can I search for any custom tag?

Yes! Search results can show you live streams using any custom tag, as long as it is an exact match. Learn more in our knowledge guide on how to search with tags: link.twitch.tv/SearchWithTags

Can I search for social media handles?

Yes! If a streamer has added their social media handles to their channel profile, they will appear in search whether online or offline. Add up to 5 social links in your channel profile settings: link.twitch.tv/3BemxRh

How to Add Stream Delay

Stream delay adds a time buffer between what happens in your broadcast and when viewers see it. This can be useful for competitive gaming, preventing stream sniping, or any other scenario where you want time between something occurring on broadcast and when it reaches your audience.

Any Twitch user can add stream delay, provided they broadcast to Twitch using software that allows users to add a stream delay.

Twitch Partners can delay their broadcast up to 15 minutes natively via the Stream Manager on Twitch, no broadcast software setting required.

Important Considerations When Using Stream Delay

Stream delay impacts real-time interaction with your chat, so consider your streaming goals before implementing a significant delay.

Broadcast software stream delay requires your software to buffer video, which increases memory usage. Stream delay managed through Twitch (Partners only) does not consume memory resources on your machine.

When stream delay is enabled, your stream won’t end immediately. It will continue for the duration of your delay.

Very long stream delays are not recommended, as they can significantly impact viewer engagement and require substantial system resources (if using broadcast software stream delay).

Adding Delay in Stream Manager (Twitch)

This feature is available to Partners only.

To add stream delay in Twitch Stream Manager:

  • Visit your Stream Manager
  • Add the Stream Delay Quick-Action
  • Set Stream Delay

Stream delay can be set up to 15 minutes.

Adding Delay in OBS Studio

OBS Studio offers a built-in stream delay feature that’s easy to configure:

  • Open OBS Studio
  • Click on Settings or Preferences
  • Select Advanced
  • Locate the Stream Delay section
  • Check Enable
  • Set your desired delay duration in seconds
  • Optionally, adjust the Preserve cutoff point setting
  • Click Apply then OK

The “Preserved cutoff point” setting determines how much of your delay buffer is preserved if your stream disconnects. This setting keeps part of your delay buffer if your connection drops, so you don’t lose footage when reconnecting.

Adding Delay in Streamlabs Desktop

To add stream delay in Streamlabs Desktop:

  • Open Streamlabs Desktop
  • Visit Settings
  • Select the Advanced tab
  • Find the Stream Delay section
  • Enable the feature and set your desired delay in seconds
  • Optionally, select Preserved cutoff point when reconnecting
  • Click Done to save your settings

Adding Delay in XSplit (Windows)

To configure stream delay in XSplit Broadcaster:

  • Open XSplit Broadcaster
  • Click on Tools in the top menu
  • Select Settings
  • Navigate to the Outputs tab
  • Find your active output (e.g., Twitch)
  • Look for the Delay option
  • Set your desired delay in seconds
  • Click OK to save your settings

Frequently Asked Questions

Why would I want to add stream delay?

A key benefit of Twitch is real-time interaction between you and your audience. However, there are situations where adding a delay between your broadcast and what viewers see can work in your favor:

  • Competitive gaming: If you’re playing competitive multiplayer games, opponents who are watching your stream could use your broadcast to gain an advantage — for example, seeing your position on a map or your strategy in real time. Adding a delay prevents this.
  • Location privacy: If you’re streaming in-person (IRL) content, a delay can help prevent viewers from knowing your exact location in real time. Keep in mind that many IRL streamers choose not to use delay because real-time interaction is central to their content — consider what works best for your situation.
  • Any scenario where real-time visibility is a concern: Whether it’s a surprise reveal, a creative project, or any content where you’d benefit from a buffer between what’s happening and what viewers see, stream delay gives you that flexibility.

For most competitive gaming scenarios, a delay of 30 to 60 seconds is common. Balance your delay against your desire to interact with chat in real time.

Will adding delay affect my stream quality?
Adding stream delay does not directly affect video or audio quality, but it does increase the memory usage of your broadcasting software (if you are using broadcast software stream delay). Ensure your computer has adequate resources if using a long delay.
Can stream delay help me avoid, censor, or delete bad audio or content on stream?
No. Stream delay simply adds a buffer of time between broadcast actions, and when the content reaches your audience. It does not allow a way to mute, bleep, or censor content in that buffer. While some traditional broadcast systems like television or radio allow for a portion of delayed audio or content to be deleted before it reaches live, this is not easily achievable by most live streaming systems. Streamers are responsible for ensuring the content that appears in their stream abides by our Terms of Service and Community Guidelines.
Can viewers tell that I’ve added a delay to my stream?
Viewers won’t receive any notification about stream delay. Regular viewers might notice the increased time between your actions and their ability to see those actions. Consider informing your audience if you’re using a significant delay.
How can I interact with chat effectively while using stream delay?
When stream delay is enabled, chat messages are responding to content you broadcast several seconds ago. Consider utilizing a second monitor or device showing your stream at the same delay viewers are experiencing, or simply be mindful of the time difference when responding to chat.
Does Twitch automatically add delay to streams?
No. While all streams have some inherent delay, Twitch does not automatically add delay to streams. Utilize Low Latency mode to minimize this natural delay.
Can I change the delay during a live stream?
In most broadcasting software, changing delay settings requires you to stop and restart your stream. Plan your delay settings before going live.

How to Appeal Muted Audio

This article explains how to appeal muted audio in VODs.

If you believe one of your videos has been incorrectly flagged by our Audio Recognition system which has resulted in a muted VOD, we offer an appeals process built into the Video Producer section of your Dashboard.

Why was my VOD muted?

Twitch services scan VODs as a proactive way to help broadcasters avoid having videos containing unauthorized audio. If copyrighted audio is detected in a VOD, we automatically mute that portion of the VOD. The fact that one of your VODs was muted does not mean that you received a DMCA notification, and muted VODs do not negatively impact your channel.

If you believe your VOD was muted in error – for example, because you own or have a license to the track(s) that led to the muting or did not play the track in your stream – and would like to have the VOD unmuted, please follow the steps outlined in How to Appeal. Please note, however, that if the muted portion of your VOD contains unauthorized copyrighted material, a person or entity that holds a copyright in that material may choose to send a notification of claimed infringement pursuant to Twitch’s DMCA Guidelines, which could lead to a strike being issued against your channel.

What you cannot appeal

You cannot appeal muted audio on the basis that you:

  • Purchased a copy of the audio or paid for access to the audio through a streaming service.
  • Buying a copy of the audio, whether in the form of a digital download, CD, vinyl record or other format, does not give you permission to make the audio available in a VOD on Twitch. Likewise, streaming audio under a personal entertainment license also does not give you permission to make the audio in a VOD on Twitch, even if you have paid for a subscription to the streaming service.
  • Credited the artist.
  • Giving credit to the artist is not enough to give you permission to make audio owned by someone other than you, available in a VOD on Twitch (unless the owner(s) of the rights have set up licensing documentation to grant authorization when crediting requirements have been met, as with certain Creative Commons licenses).

How to appeal

  • Click on the dropdown menu of video you would like to appeal. Videos with muted audio have a red muted speaker icon in the upper right corner of the thumbnail.
  • Find the audio track(s) you would like to appeal.
  • Choose the reason for the appeal:
  • My video does not contain the audio identified.
  • I created and performed the original music without including any third party audio, and own all the rights.
  • I have permission from all applicable rights holders to use the audio and distribute it on Twitch as part of my video.
  • My use of the audio as part of my video on Twitch is fair use.
  • Confirm the audio you have selected to appeal with the Appeal Selected button.
  • Attest that you have the right to use the flagged audio and submit, along with your legal full name and address.
  • Submit your appeal by clicking Submit.

You will receive a confirmation screen and email after submitting your appeal. You can check the status of your appeal by clicking on the appealed video where you will see either Unmuted or Denied. When your video has been reviewed, you will receive an email with the outcome of your appeal.

If you already have a muted video in appeal, you should not submit a new appeal. We will respond to your original appeal (and all appeals) in the order in which it was received.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are some ways to avoid getting my content flagged and muted?
To learn more about what music content is allowed in VODs, please refer to our Music Guidelines.
Will my live content be flagged or muted?
No, this appeals process is strictly for VOD content.

How to Create, Edit, and Share Clips

Did anyone clip that?! Clips allow you and your viewers to capture and share the most uniquely Twitch moments from broadcasts. Post clips of your top stream moments to social media to give new viewers a sense of what your channel is all about and bring them back to your next stream.

  • When a clip is created, we auto-generate a portrait version of the clip next to your landscape clip. Landscape clips are best for web, while portrait versions are optimized for mobile. Your portrait clip is automatically cropped to keep your cam and gameplay in frame, and you can accept, adjust, or dismiss the suggestion.
  • The clip creator opens as a moveable overlay. You can continue watching your stream while capturing key moments. If you prefer the previous clipping experience, you can switch back using the toggle in the top-right of the clip creator.
  • It’s easy to capture great clips for mobile viewing. Edit the portrait layout of any clip once to auto-generate portrait clips to this layout. We follow your portrait layout preference for all future clips made of your channel by you or your viewers. You can adjust layout preferences at any time, as we will default to your latest preference.
  • Once the channel owner edits or features a clip, the original viewer cannot make changes to it. This prevents changes being made to clips you have already chosen to feature.
  • Viewers can now comment on your clips. Comments let your community react to and discuss your best moments with threaded conversations. Safety protections are on by default, and you can manage access or disable comments in your Clips Settings. Learn more about Comments on Clips.

Read on to learn how to create and manage clips, edit them for vertical formats, and share them to social media to promote and grow your channel.

On this page:

  • How to Create Clips
  • About Clips Leaderboard
  • How to Manage Clips
  • How to Edit Clips
  • How to Share Clips
  • Frequently Asked Questions

How to Create Clips

Creating a clip is fast, and preparing it to share on social media is easy. Plus, you can create clips without leaving the stream you’re watching

  • Click the clip icon (shown above) on a live stream or past broadcast to open the Clip Creator. (If watching on mobile, you may need to tap the video for the icon to appear).
  • The Clip Creator opens as a movable overlay on the channel page, allowing you to continue watching the stream while creating your clip. You can reposition the Clip Creator anywhere on the page by clicking and dragging the top bar of the overlay.
  • Adjust the length of the clip you’d like to create, up to 60 seconds, by using the slider underneath the video player.
  • Review your layout and crop suggestion. Learn more. When you open the clip editor, you’ll see a suggested crop that keeps your cam and gameplay in frame. This works by automatically detecting where your camera and gameplay appear in your stream to suggest the best frame, and does not store face data or perform facial recognition. You can also choose any aspect ratio from landscape (16:9) to portrait (9:16). Accept the suggestion, adjust it, or dismiss it — it’s your clip. If your cam or gameplay can’t be confidently identified, you’ll see a centered crop as a starting point.
  • Once you’ve selected the right moment, give your clip a title and click Publish.

When you open the Clip Creator, the stream audio will automatically be muted so you can focus on the clip audio. You can unmute the stream if needed, but be aware that both audio sources will play simultaneously.

If you try to navigate away from the page while creating a clip, you’ll receive a browser prompt reminding you to save your clip first.

At clip creation, streamers, editors, and eligible moderators can choose to feature a clip. Additionally, streamers control whether a clip can be exported directly to social media accounts, or whether they wish to add that clip to their Stream Recap.

Create Clips with Your Voice

You can also create clips using your voice while streaming. Say “Twitch, Clip That” out loud during your live broadcast, and Twitch will automatically create a clip for you.

  • During your livestream, when a moment happens that you want to say, say “Twitch, Clip That” out loud.
  • Twitch captures the moment and generates a clip automatically
  • You’ll receive a notification letting you know if a clip was generated successfully
  • Your clip appears in your Clips Manager, ready to review, edit, or share

Congrats, you clipped it! You’ll receive a clip URL to copy and share your clip with others. You can also directly post your clip from Twitch to TikTok, Youtube, Instagram, or Snapchat to reach a wider audience of potential viewers.

About Clips Leaderboard

Streamers can enable a Clips Leaderboard in their channel to showcase the most popular clips being created. Channel owners can manage their leaderboard settings here. Learn more.

Manage Clips in the Clips Manager

Click here to visit your Clips Manager. In your Clips Manager, you can:

  • Find your clips, fast - Use the search box to find your clips by title or category. You can also filter for clips by category, who it was clipped by, date range, or if the clip is featured.
  • Edit clips you’ve made, clips made by others, and clips you’ve made of other channels – You can re-edit the title, trim, or portrait layout, or add/remove captions of any clips of your own channel by clicking the scissor icon. Once you make edits to clips of your channel, the original clip creator cannot make changes. You can also edit clips you’ve made of other channels, so long as the channel owner has not edited or featured that clip.
  • Delete clips you’ve made, clips made by others, and clips you’ve made of other channels – You can always delete clips of your channel. You can delete clips you’ve made of other channels, so long as the channel owner has not edited or featured that clip.
  • Share your clips, clips made by others, and clips you’ve made of other channels - You can directly post clips to your YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat accounts, or share a URL to the clip on other social media platforms. For clips you’ve made of other channels, if the streamer has the setting turned on, you will be able to directly post their clips to social media.

Some actions like sharing, featuring, or editing clips are impacted by clip settings you set, or set by the clipped channel.

The scissor icon lets you re-edit the title, trim, or portrait layout of any clips of your channel at any time. Learn more.

You can toggle captions on or off, or edit the caption text, for clips of your channel within 30 days of creation. After 30 days, captions are locked. Clips created via the Clip That Quick Action or Auto Clips include captions by default. For other clips, captions are included if “Add Captions” was selected at creation. Streamers can disable default captions for Auto Clips through Creator Dashboard > Settings > Stream > Clips Settings.

The scissor icon lets you re-edit the title, trim, or portrait layout of any clips you created of someone else’s channel, up until the channel owner edits, features or exports the clip themselves

Feature Clip
