Enabling Past Broadcast (VOD) Storage

After you stream, you can find your broadcast in your Video Producer to review it, create Highlights and Clips, or download it. To make sure your broadcasts are saved, confirm that Past Broadcast storage is turned on in your Stream Settings.

Most Twitch Partners, Prime and Twitch Turbo users will have their past broadcasts saved for 60 days before being deleted. Affiliate broadcasts are saved for 14 days. All other broadcasters will have their past broadcasts saved for 7 days before they are deleted.

If the Store Past Broadcasts toggle is turned off, your past broadcasts won’t be saved, and you won’t be able to create Highlights or Clips from them. Confirm this setting is turned on before you go live to save past broadcasts.

The Store Past Broadcasts setting can only be enabled through the Creator Dashboard on web. This setting is not available in the Twitch mobile app. If you stream from your phone, you must enable this setting on web first — otherwise your mobile broadcasts will not be saved.

If your stream configurations are not set up properly or your network is unstable, streams might not save even if the Store Past Broadcasts toggle is on. To troubleshoot, use Twitch Inspector. Our help article on Broadcast Health and how to use Twitch Inspector can help you find recommended settings and requirements depending on your streaming needs and device capabilities.

Twitch Support cannot recover a broadcast that was not saved. If Store Past Broadcasts was not enabled before you went live, or if your stream did not save due to incompatible configurations, the content does not exist on Twitch’s servers and cannot be retrieved. Always confirm this setting is enabled before starting your stream.

Please note that once you turn on past broadcast storage, past broadcasts will be published as VODs by default, except for VODs of streams broadcast in your Excluded Categories, and if you have disabled the setting Always Publish VODs. If you disable this toggle, or add an Excluded Category, you will need to review these VODs before publishing them.

The Video Producer

You can manage your Past Broadcasts (VODs), Highlights and Uploads using the Video Producer, and it’s also where you can go to see your copyright strike status. To get there, go to your Creator Dashboard, then select Video Producer under the Content dropdown menu.

On this screen, you can use the drop-down menu on the left above the video list to filter by video type. You can also sort the videos by date created, length of video, and view count.

You can also track your Highlights and Uploads storage, as well as the number of copyright strikes on your account in the panels on the right side of the Video Producer.

How to Manage Your Videos and Storage

Download Videos

To download your videos, click the 3 Vertical Dots menu icon next to any individual video to open a menu with a wider set of options. Click download to save a video to your local device.

Twitch does not offer the option to bulk download your videos, but some third-party tools are available that allow bulk-downloads.

Please note that depending on the length of the video, it may take an extended period of time for this download to start. If your video has been muted due to the Audio Recognition system, downloading it will not provide an unmuted version of the video. For more information about appealing muted audio, please see our help article.

Export Videos

Your Twitch account can be connected to a YouTube account via your Connections page. Once your accounts are connected, you can use the Export option to upload your videos to YouTube directly from Twitch without having to download them locally. Tip: To be able to upload VODs past the 15 min upload limit on YouTube, make sure you verify your YouTube account.

Delete Videos

Use the filters to filter by content type if you are trying to delete just Highlights or Uploads to free up storage space. You can sort your videos by least viewed, date created, and length of video to help decide which content may free up the most space.

When deleting videos in the video producer, you’ll be able to see how many hours of storage you will regain by deleting selected content before you hit delete.

Unpublish or Publish Videos

All VODs are published by default if past VOD storage is enabled. Unpublishing a video will make it publicly inaccessible.

You can unpublish or publish individual videos using the 3 Vertical Dots menu. To unpublish or publish videos in bulk, select the videos you want to manage using the check boxes on the left side of the video producer and then select unpublish or publish.

Reminder: Both Published and Unpublished Highlights and Uploads count towards your storage limit. Unpublishing Highlights or Uploads will not free up storage space. You must delete Highlights or Uploads to free storage space.

Edit

Clicking the Edit option from the 3 Vertical Dots menu will bring up the edit panel. Clicking on a specific video listing will also bring up the edit panel. You’ll have the option on this panel to edit the Title, Description, Language and Category for a video. You can also remove tags, adjust the video thumbnail or edit the permissions for who can view your video.

After you’ve finished editing your video, click Save Changes. Clicking Cancel will revert all changes.

Add to

Clicking on Add to will bring up another two options:

Collection

Collections are playlists which let you organize and show off your best work. You can create Collections for any set of videos you want to highlight on your channel, whether it is a general introduction reel, a recurring show, each game you stream, or creative projects that span across multiple streams on your channel. For more information about collections and making a collection, please see our help article.

Rerun Queue

Reruns are non-live content that you can play on your channel. To broadcast a Rerun, you can capture and stream your VODs from your streaming encoder of choice. Make sure to let your viewers know when you’re broadcasting pre-recorded content by following these three steps:

  • Select the “Rerun” checkbox in the Edit Stream Info panel
  • Add “[Rerun]” to the beginning of your Stream Title
  • Add “[Rerun]” to the beginning of your Go Live Notification copy

Selecting the Rerun checkbox adds a Rerun tag to your stream. Failing to properly label your stream as a Rerun can damage community trust. Without the Rerun label, your viewers expect to engage with a live streamer. Streamers who are properly broadcasting a Rerun will display a Rerun label on their channel page.

Highlight

This option is available on Past Broadcasts. Selecting it will bring you to the Highlighter. Here, you can create Highlights. You may not be able to create new Highlights if you are at or close to the 100-hour storage limit. Delete Highlights or Uploads to free up space to make more Highlights. For more information on creating Highlights, please see our dedicated help article for Highlights.

Watch

Click this to watch your published VODs in a new tab. You can also click directly on the row for a specific VOD to watch it in your Video Producer. Both published and unpublished VODs can be easily watched right inside your Video Producer.

Video Chapters

When you change the category of your stream while live, we automatically save that information for you as chapters. On playback, viewers can jump to the timestamp of your category change. There is no way to modify category change information after they are created.

Frequently Asked Questions
Do my Past Broadcasts (VODs) count towards my storage limit?
No. Only content classified as Highlights or Uploads count towards your storage limit. If you were previously storing full VODs as Highlights, please note that these are stored as Highlights and will count towards your limit.
Can I bulk download my Highlights or uploads before deleting any content?
Unfortunately it is not possible to bulk download Highlights and Uploads. You can only download or export content one at a time. While Twitch doesn’t offer the ability to bulk download, some third-party tools are available that allow you to download your Highlights and Uploads with less manual work. We hope that by giving you two months notice, you and/or your editors can take your time to manage your existing storage limit.
Can I bulk delete my Highlights or Uploads?
Yes, it is possible to delete in bulk once you’ve decided which Highlights or Uploads you’d like to remove. Remember, you do not need to remove all of your content – only enough to bring you under the 100-hour limit.
Can my editor help download, export, and delete my Highlights and Uploads?
Yes.
What can I use now instead of Highlights and Uploads if I want to store all of my VODs beyond the current storage period of Twitch?
You can download your VODs to store them locally, or you can connect your Twitch account to YouTube to export and save your VODs directly to your YouTube account. Please view this help article to learn how you can download and export VODs, Highlights, and Uploads.
Can Twitch Support recover a VOD that wasn’t saved?
No. If your broadcast was not saved — either because Store Past Broadcasts was not enabled, your stream had incompatible configurations, or the VOD has passed its retention period — the content no longer exists on Twitch’s servers and cannot be recovered by Twitch Support. To protect your content, enable Store Past Broadcasts in your Stream Settings before going live, and download important VODs before they expire.

PlayStation Broadcasting

PlayStation broadcasting is managed by Sony. For detailed setup instructions, troubleshooting, and technical support, visit PlayStation Support.

SUPPORT SCOPE: PlayStation broadcasting functionality is managed by Sony, not Twitch. Twitch Support cannot troubleshoot PlayStation console streaming issues, PlayStation OS updates, or PlayStation hardware problems. Direct all PlayStation broadcasting questions to PlayStation Support at playstation.com

PlayStation consoles include a built-in broadcast feature that lets you stream directly to Twitch. To get started, check out Twitch Creator Camp: Stream on PlayStation for an overview of the experience.

How to Broadcast From Your PlayStation

PlayStation 5:

  • Press the Create button on your DualSense controller
  • Select Broadcast
  • Choose Twitch and follow the prompts to link your account

For complete PS5 setup instructions, visit PlayStation 5 Broadcast Support.

PlayStation 4:

  • Press the Share button on your DualShock controller
  • Select Broadcast Gameplay
  • Choose Twitch and follow the prompts to link your account

For complete PS4 setup instructions, visit PlayStation 4 Broadcast Support.

Console broadcasting streams your gameplay directly without overlays, alerts, or other interactive stream elements. For a more customized streaming experience with overlays and scene transitions, consider using a capture card connected to a streaming PC with software like OBS. Visit Twitch Creator Camp to learn more about your options.

Party Chat and Audio

If party chat audio is not being included in your broadcast, check the following:

  • Ensure your PlayStation system software is fully updated
  • Check your privacy settings to confirm voice chat sharing is enabled
  • Review your volume settings for party chat

For more detailed audio troubleshooting, see PlayStation’s guide on troubleshooting audio problems in parties.

Some PlayStation security settings may prevent audio from being shared in broadcasts. PlayStation Support can provide the most insight into their product’s privacy and audio sharing settings.

Troubleshooting

PlayStation broadcasting issues: For problems with console streaming, system updates, network connectivity, party chat, or hardware issues, contact PlayStation Support.

Twitch account linking issues: If you’re having trouble linking your Twitch account to your PlayStation, try unlinking and relinking from your Twitch Connections settings.

Twitch stream key issues: If you need to reset your stream key, go to your Creator Dashboard > Settings > Stream and click Reset. Only reset once to avoid a 15-minute lockout.

Pokémon Chat Badge Drops Campaign

In this Pokémon Chat Badge Drops Campaign guide, we’ll explain what’s unique about this Drops campaign, so you know what to expect and how to make progress toward the rewards you want. If you’re troubleshooting a specific issue (progress not counting, a Poké Ball not opening, or a missing reward), see our Drops Troubleshooting guide instead.

This campaign is available on live channels streaming in participating categories (see Where to Watch). Open the Drops & More panel in chat on one of those channels to see the campaign and track your progress.

Check out our official announcement for full details and Terms and Conditions.

How It Works

Pokémon Chat Badges are released in limited-time windows. For each badge:

  • Earn a Poké Ball. Depending on the window, you earn one by watching or by subscribing to a channel in a participating category.
  • Open it by watching. Watch participating channels for 20 minutes a day on 3 different days to unlock the badge inside. See Opening Poké Balls.
  • Equip and evolve. Equip your badge and keep watching to earn its evolved forms. See Evolving Your Badges.

Once a window closes, its badges can no longer be earned, but badges you’ve already earned stay in your Pokémon Collection. To see all active Drops campaigns of any kind, visit the Drops campaigns page.

Where to Watch

Watch or subscribe to any live channel streaming in one of these categories:

  • Pokémon games: Pokémon FireRed/LeafGreen, Pokémon Pokopia, Pokémon UNITE, Pokémon Champions, Pokémon GO, Pokémon Legends: Z-A, Pokémon Scarlet/Violet, Pokémon Trading Card Game Pocket, Pokémon Trading Card Game, Pokémon Trading Card Game Live, and Pokémon Diamond/Pearl
  • Other categories: Just Chatting, DJs, Art, Special Events, Sports, Music, Talk Shows & Podcasts, Animals, Aquariums, and Zoos, Co-working & Studying, and Makers & Crafting

To find participating channels, look for the Drops Enabled tag on channels in these categories. To confirm a channel counts, open the Drops & More panel in chat and check that the Pokémon campaign appears. You don’t need to connect a game account to earn Pokémon Chat Badges.

Pokémon Night Out Campaign (October 16-24, 2026)

To celebrate Pokémon Night Out, you can earn the Gastly chat badge and evolve it into Haunter and Gengar.

How to Earn Gastly

  • Between 10:00 PT on October 16 and 23:59 PT on October 24, 2026, subscribe or gift a subscription to a channel in a participating category. You’ll earn a Pokémon Night Out Themed Poké Ball (a type of Special Poké Ball) that holds Gastly.

  • Watch participating channels for 20 minutes a day for 3 days to open it and unlock Gastly.

  • Equip Gastly and keep watching to evolve it into Haunter, then into Gengar. See Evolving Your Badges.

  • Gastly is only available by subscribing or gifting a subscription. Watching alone doesn’t earn it.

  • You can earn 1 Pokémon Night Out Themed Poké Ball, from your first qualifying subscription or gift.

  • When you gift a subscription, you earn the Poké Ball. Gift recipients don’t.

  • Prime subscriptions and renewals of an existing subscription don’t count. If you’re already subscribed to a channel, subscribe to a different participating channel or gift a subscription instead.

Key Dates (Pokémon Night Out and First Partners Campaigns)
  • October 24, 2026 (23:59 PT): Last day to earn your Pokémon Night Out Themed Poké Ball. Complete at least 1 day of watch progress on it by then, or you won’t be able to open it after the window ends.
  • October 31, 2026 (23:59 PT): Last day to open any Poké Ball or Great Ball from the First Partners Campaign and unlock Pichu, Bulbasaur, Squirtle, or Charmander.
  • November 23, 2026: Last day to finish opening your Pokémon Night Out Themed Poké Ball and unlock Gastly.
  • January 30, 2027: Last day to evolve badges from both the First Partners and Pokémon Night Out campaigns.

Opening Poké Balls

A Poké Ball holds a Pokémon Chat Badge. To open it, watch participating channels for 20 minutes a day on 3 different days. This is called Daily Watch Progress.

How You Earn Poké Balls
  • Normal Poké Balls are earned by watching a participating channel, when a badge window includes one.
  • Special Poké Balls, such as the Great Ball and the Pokémon Night Out Themed Poké Ball, are earned by subscribing (or gift subscribing) to a participating channel. Gift recipients don’t earn one. Prime subscriptions and renewals of an existing subscription don’t count.
Multiple Poké Balls

You can hold more than one Poké Ball, but only one of each type (normal and Special) makes progress at a time. The next one starts once the current one opens. Special Poké Balls in the same window each hold a different badge, so you won’t get duplicates.

How Daily Watch Progress Works
  • Watch any participating channel. You don’t need to watch the same channel every day.
  • Days don’t need to be consecutive.
  • A “day” is a rolling 24-hour window that starts when you begin watching toward that reward, so one day’s requirement may span two calendar dates.
  • If you don’t finish the 20 minutes before that day ends, that day’s progress resets. Days you’ve already completed aren’t affected.

Check your progress, and how much time is left in your current day, in the Drops & More panel on any participating channel.

Daily Watch Progress is different from Watch Streaks. Watch Streaks track consecutive days of watching a specific streamer for a loyalty reward. Daily Watch Progress tracks cumulative days (not necessarily consecutive) toward a campaign reward and can apply across any participating channel.

Evolving Your Badges

Once you’ve earned a Pokémon Chat Badge, you can evolve it by watching. You don’t need to subscribe again.

How to Evolve a Badge
  • In chat on a participating channel, open the Drops & More panel.
  • Under Watch Drops, select Swap and choose the badge you want to equip. Evolution progress only counts while the badge is equipped.
  • Watch participating channels for 20 minutes a day for 3 days. Days don’t need to be consecutive. Track your progress in the Drops & More panel.
  • You unlock the evolved form as an additional badge, and you keep the earlier one.
  • To evolve it again, use Swap to equip the new badge and repeat.
Evolution Lines
  • Pichu → Pikachu
  • Bulbasaur → Ivysaur → Venusaur
  • Squirtle → Wartortle → Blastoise
  • Charmander → Charmeleon → Charizard
  • Gastly → Haunter → Gengar

You can evolve these badges until January 30, 2027. After that, you won’t be able to unlock more badges in the evolution line.

First Partners Campaign: Pichu, Bulbasaur, Squirtle, and Charmander

The First Partners Campaign ran from August 24 to October 1, 2026. Subscribing earned a Great Ball holding Bulbasaur, Squirtle, or Charmander, and watching earned a Poké Ball holding Pichu. These badges can no longer be earned, but if you have one, you can evolve it starting October 16, 2026.

If you still have an unopened Poké Ball or Great Ball from this campaign, finish opening it by October 31, 2026.

Pokémon Collection

Your Pokémon Collection tracks your progress toward campaign rewards. This is different from Collections in Video Producer, which let you organize your videos into playlists.

Your Pokémon Collection shows which campaign rewards you’ve unlocked and which ones you can still earn.

  • Only rewards that are actually obtainable by you appear in your Pokémon Collection - you won’t see empty slots for items that aren’t available to earn.
  • Once you claim a reward, it’s added to your Pokémon Collection automatically.
How to View Your Pokémon Collection

Your Pokémon Collection is located on your badge panel.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I choose which Pokémon Chat Badge I get when I unlock a Special Poké Ball?
No. Special Poké Ball contents are selected from the pool of available badges - you can’t select a specific one. You won’t receive a duplicate, though: each Special Poké Ball you earn in a window gives you a badge you don’t have yet.
Is this Pokémon campaign on Twitch official?
Yes. Twitch and The Pokémon Company are officially collaborating on this campaign. The campaign runs as a series of badge windows over time rather than a single event, and each window has its own rewards and Terms and Conditions. Visit our official announcement for full details and Terms and Conditions.
Do I need to subscribe again to evolve my badges?
No. Evolving a badge only requires watching. Equip the badge and watch participating channels for 20 minutes a day for 3 days. See Evolving Your Badges.

Reactions on Clips

Reactions on clips is a way for users to engage with the community and provide feedback to creators on their clips through 5 different emotes. Streamers can choose to keep the 4 preset global Twitch emotes or can customize each reaction with their own custom channel emotes. The 5 reactions for clips are: Like, love, hype, laugh, and sad.

How to React to Clips

Reactions on clips are available to all users on both the mobile apps (Android and iOS) and the web. For a quick reaction on mobile, simply double-tap the screen to send a like. To access more emotes, press and hold the like button to choose from a wider selection. On the web, hover over the like button to reveal additional emote options, giving you more ways to react beyond just a like.

Customized Reactions

The 5 preset global emotes for the reactions include:

  • Thumbs up (Like)
  • :bleedpurple: (Love)
  • :curselit: (Hype)
  • :lul: (Laugh)
  • :tearglove: (Sad)

Channel owners can replace 4 of the 5 global preset emotes with custom emotes from their own channel. Like will not be able to be customized and will remain a thumbs up across all channels, while the love, hype, laugh, and sad reactions can be swapped and customized. While the emotes themselves can be changed, the assigned reaction slot will remain fixed.

Streamers: How to Customize Your Reactions

To customize reactions to your channel’s clips with your channel emotes, begin by logging in to your Twitch account and click into settings in your Creator Dashboard.

  • Click Stream Settings
  • Scroll down to Clip Reactions
  • Click ‘Edit’ under the emotes you wish to swap out

Frequently Asked Questions

How can I see the list of emotes I can react with?
While on the app, a long press on the thumbs up button will open a list of emote options to react with. While on desktop, users will be able to hover over the thumbs up button to reveal the list of emotes.
Why can’t I find a clip I reacted to?
When a clip is deleted, the reactions associated with the clip are deleted as well.
Am I able to react to a clip multiple times?
No, users are only allowed to react once per clip. However, users are able to change which emote to react with.
How can I see other reactions on clips?
To see the list of other reactions on a clip on mobile, click on the 3 dots in the bottom right corner of the screen. Here you will find the option to view reactions under the “View Reactions” option. On the web, you can view other Reactions by clicking on the down arrow next to the like count. This will bring you to the “View Reactions” option. Click on “View Reactions” to see the list of Reactions.

Research Analytics

The Research Analytics page surfaces global Twitch data beyond just your channel analytics to help you plan upcoming streams. We aim to add more data to this page to refine your research.

What’s in my Research Analytics?

Your Research Analytics page contains the following information:

  • Time to Stream - This panel provides data on the average viewers per channel, average viewers, and average channels live at different hours & days of the week to help you plan the best time to stream. You can filter by viewer, region, category (game type), and streamer language.
    • Exclude popular channels – A popular channel is a channel that is trending in the top 2% of the category’s concurrent viewership at that hour, and at minimum averages 100 or more viewers.

Frequently Asked Questions

What else can I learn with Analytics?

Dive in by visiting your Research Analytics, or click here for an overview.

Where can I leave feedback on Analytics?

Browse the pages and let us know your suggestions or feedback in UserVoice.

Setting Up Third-Party Events on Twitch

New to Twitch’s Alerts? Visit our start-up guide here.

Recently, we’ve integrated useful third-party functions into Twitch’s Alerts, Activity Feed, and Chat & Events. In this guide, learn how to set up, authorize, and configure third-party events into Twitch’s Alerts and other streamer tools.

What Are Third-Party Events?

Twitch’s Alerts, your Activity Feed, and Chat & Events drive awareness of new Follows, Subscribers, and much more. However, some streamers use additional tools and services to drive this customization further. As a result, Twitch’s Alerts, your Activity Feed, and Chat & Events have been updated to allow you the flexibility to configure key third-party events into your stream.

Third-party events are events that originate from services that are not Twitch. To use third-party events, you must have an account with that service, and authorize it to connect with your Twitch account. Third-party events are safe to use when connected to your Twitch account through the steps in this guide. You should use them if you think it would be a good fit for your stream.

Hey developers - want to see your events in Twitch’s Alerts? Contact us here.

Connecting Your Accounts

To use third-party events with Twitch’s Alerts, connect your Twitch account and the service used. You can connect some third-party services to your Twitch account via the Streaming Tools page on Twitch, or while setting up Alerts.

New to Twitch’s Alerts? Visit our start-up guide here.

  • Visit your Creator Dashboard -> Alerts
  • Create an Alert Box, or Edit an existing Alert Box
  • Select Connect to log into the third-party service
  • Complete the authentication process between Twitch and the service to continue

Third-Party Event Alert Variants

Within each third-party event alert, you can create “variants,” which are specific alerts based on various conditions selected. When creating or editing a third-party event, it is important to set the Alert Condition.

For example, if you set up your account to use Streamlabs events, you can create a specific alert for Media Shares, Items Purchased, or Donations reached, each of which would contain their own images, sounds, and animations.

Third-Party Events in Chat & Events

Third-party alerts can be configured in Chat & Events, allowing you even more control of how you manage your stream.

Learn more about Chat & Events here.

Setting Up Twitch’s Alerts

Alerts are core to the streaming experience. They highlight your communities’ actions driving awareness of what happened and who did it while forging a stronger bond. Activating and customizing alerts help you communicate your unique brand, stand out from the pack, and build a deeper relationship with your audience.

Alerts can now be set up directly from your Creator Dashboard with a few simple steps! We have everything you need to create compelling alerts that your communities will love.

Setting Up Alerts

Partners and Affiliates can earn 2 additional animated emote slots for 60 days if they use Twitch’s Alerts. Learn more.

You can enable alerts by going to the Alerts page within the Creator Dashboard. Once there, you will be prompted to Create Alert Set.

You can think of an alert set as a collection of all of the alerts you would like to show on your video feed including subscribing, following, raiding, hype trains, and much more! Name your set and add a description.

Alert sets can come in handy if you want your alerts to look different for different games you stream or for the holidays. They can also allow you to have one set of alerts displayed in one location of your stream and another set to be located elsewhere.

Alert sets can be easily turned on / off, using the toggles, as you need them once the browser source is copied to your broadcasting software, as well as deleted and renamed.

Alert Variants

If you want to see what your alert will look like, use the Preview Alert to test it.

Click Edit Alerts on the desired alert set. You will be navigated to the alerts editor page, allowing you to start editing your alert set.

Once in the alerts editor, the left-hand side contains a list of all of the events you can create alerts for. This includes Follows, Subscriptions, Hype Train, Goals, Charity, Raids, Cheering, and more! Within each event, you can create “variants,” which are specific alerts based on various conditions selected For example, you can create a specific alert for 6-month subscribers that’s different from an alert for 2-month subscribers, each of which would contain their own images, sounds, and animations. Default variants are available for each alert event.

Check out our Types of Twitch’s Alerts article for more information about variants and conditions for specific alert events.

To create a new variant, click the New Variant option under the type of alert you want to add. If preferred, you can also start from a pre-made default alert variant by clicking on any of the options above. When creating or editing a variant, the most important setting to enable is the Alert Condition.

The alert condition is the logic that determines when the alert will surface. For example, for a Subscriptions alert, a condition of “Months subscribed exactly” with a “Months” of “1” means that the alert will only surface for 1-month/new subs. The list of conditions available changes depending on the alert event.

Once you’ve named and specified the condition for your alert variant, you can customize several different options to make your alerts unique!

For more details about the options available for alert variants, check out our Twitch’s Alerts Customization article.

Organizing Variants

As mentioned previously, variants allow you to create alerts for all conditions, such as different alerts for a 1-month sub versus a 9-month subscription. But what happens if someone qualifies for multiple alert conditions, such as a Prime-Sub and a 1-month sub? That’s where variant priority comes into play! To organize your variant priority, renumber or drag-and-drop variants within a category. Variants higher in priority will show first in the case of overlapping conditions.

In this example, if someone is both a New Subscription and a Prime Subscription, the alert for New Subscription will show on the screen. You can have up to 100 variants within an alert set.

As a general rule of thumb, the more specific the variant, the higher in priority it should be. For example, if I have an alert for “All Subscribers” and a separate alert for “2-Month Subscribers,” the “2-Month Subscribers” is more specific and should be higher in priority. Otherwise, the “All Subscribers” alert will show for 2-month subs.

Alert variants can also easily be deactivated or activated by toggling them.

Randomizing Alerts

You may wish to randomly cycle between multiple alert variations when triggered on your stream. To do this, you can Randomize alerts variations of the same event type and Alert Condition.

  • From your Alerts page, select the Alerts Box you wish to update.
  • Choose the event type whose variants you wish to randomize
  • Make sure you have created at least two variants with matching Alert Conditions
  • Select Randomize

Now, a random variant alert will trigger when the conditions are met, based on the Chance you set. You can tell which alerts are included in the randomization from the icon next to them in the events list.

If you don’t already have variants eligible for randomization, you can Create Randomized Duplicate from the general settings of an alert variant. This duplicates your current variant, and enables randomization in one step.

When randomization is enabled, the list order of your variants will change. With randomization, alerts appear grouped by condition, so you can see which variants are going to be randomized against each other.

Some Alert Conditions require a second field for additional parameters. Both fields must exactly match each other to randomize.

Will Randomize

Won’t Randomize

Two subscriptions alerts, each with the same exact conditions:

  • “Months subscribed at least”
  • Secondary - “Months: 1”

Two subscription event alerts, each with the same Alert Condition, but different secondary condition:

  • “Months subscribed at least”
  • “First alert -”Months: 1”
  • Second alert - “Months: 2”

Chance allows you to mix up randomization. Below is an example of how often you can expect each chance of alert to trigger, if one variant of each chance is set up for certain conditions.

Chance

Meaning

Common

1000 times more likely than Ultra

Uncommon

300 times more likely than Ultra

Rare

100 times more likely than Ultra

Super Rare

20 times more likely than Ultra

Ultra Rare

Appears based on Alert Condition

If you create multiple alerts with overlapping Alert Conditions, we will pick the more specific variant when a trigger occurs.

  • For example, say you have two alerts active: “Months subscribed, At least 2” and “Months subscribed, At least 6.” If a 12-month subscription is purchased in your channel, and randomization is enabled for subscription events, we pick the more specific trigger of At least 6 (depending on Chance).
  • Another example, say you have two alerts active: “Exactly 150 Bits cheered” and “At least 100 Bits cheered.” If a 150-Bit cheer is made, and randomization is enabled for Cheering events, we pick the more specific trigger of Exactly 150 Bits (depending on Chance).

In general, if randomized alerts are not appearing as often as expected, consider adjusting your specific Alert Conditions, and Chance for each variant.

Enabling Browser Source

Once you’ve created your alert set, you will need to enable the set in your broadcasting software by way of a Browser Source. This is a unique URL created for every alert set that is added as a source within your broadcasting software. It is essentially a webpage that can render your alert set when the conditions you’ve set are met. To enable your alert set browser source, copy the URL from the bottom right corner of the editing view and paste it into your broadcasting software.

You can also copy the browser source by clicking on the triple-dot menu on the alert set itself.

To ensure that your alerts look the exact same in your broadcasting software as they do in the editor, make sure the dimensions of the browser source are the same as in the alerts editor.

You only need to copy over the browser source for an alert set once. Now, whenever you make changes to the alert set in Creator Dashboard, the saved changes will reflect on stream! To test this, try Send Test Alert to ensure that things are hooked up correctly.

You can also now completely deactivate alerts by toggling off the set itself in Creator Dashboard.

Deleting Alerts

Deleting an alert variant or an alert set cannot be undone. So make sure you want it deleted before confirming. Go into the alert variant you want to delete. Scroll to the bottom of the Settings on the right and toggle open the DANGER ZONE section. Click on the red Delete Variant button to delete that alert variant.

Deleting a variant cannot be undone.

Deleting Alert Sets

To delete an alert set, navigate to the alert settings page and click the Vertical Dots menu icon on the respective alert set.

Then, select Delete and confirm. You may receive a warning if an existing Alerts layer currently selects the alert set you are deleting.

If you delete an alert set, there is no way to undo that action. To get that alert set back, you must reconfigure it from the default settings or an existing alert set.

Bulk Edit & Duplicate

Looking for a fast way to update a setting across dozens of variants? We’ve got you covered with bulk edit! Simply click on Edit Multiple above the alert events and select the variants you would like to update at once.

You can also preview specific variants before saving by selecting the variant from the Preview Alert dropdown.

If you would rather just copy an entire alert to make small changes, then try Duplicate instead. This will create a copy of the selected variant.

Activity Feed

As part of your Activity Feed, you can now also manage your alerts as well. To do so, simply turn on Live Alerts Controls from the Alerts page in Creator Dashboard.

You can also turn them on by going into the Stream Manager. In the Activity Feed click on the Filter, and select the Alerts tab.

Enabling Live Alerts Controls provides the following capabilities:

Controls

Description

Skip Alert

Ability to skip the active or upcoming alerts.

Replay Alert

Ability to replay an alert.

Enable/Disable Alerts

Ability to enable or disable specific alerts from surfacing.

Do Not Disturb

Ability to immediately disable all active and upcoming alerts.

Every alert you create will have a corresponding Activity Feed event to skip, replay, and disable if available.

Stream Manager

Stream Manager is the control panel for your stream.

Stream Manager Overview

Stream Manager is fully customizable; you can add, remove, resize or reposition the stats and panels to match your workflow. You can even create up to 5 different layouts with different customizations that you can access at any time.

To do this:
  • In the top left corner of your Stream Manager, click on the drop-down arrow to the right of Stream Manager and select Create New Layout to create a new layout. Name your layout and click Save. Then, click on the drop-down arrow again, and select Edit in order to choose which stats and panels you’d like to appear in your layout.
  • After you select Edit, you will see a + icon appear on the right edge of the page. Hover your cursor over the + icon to slide open the Edit Stream Manager Layout menu. To add different panels to your Stream Manager, you can either drag and drop them directly where you want to place them in your layout, or you can click on the + icon at the right of each panel. To remove a panel after it’s been added, click on the X icon at the top right corner of the panel, or drag the panel towards a trash can icon that will appear at the right edge of the page. You can always choose to return your layout to the default settings by clicking on the drop-down menu at the top left corner of the page and selecting Reset to Default.
  • Make sure to click Save in the top left to save your settings!

Stream Manager Panels

Activity Feed

Activity Feed Panels help you monitor new follows, subscriptions, some third-party events, and Cheers so you can recognize your viewers in chat and deepen your relationship with your community while you stream.

Click the 3 Horizontal Dots in the top right-hand corner of the panel to adjust the type of activity you want to appear in your Activity Feed, as well as to enable Popout Mode. You can create up to 4 Activity Feed panels, each with their own filter setting, making it easier to hone in on specific activities, such as only Subs and only follows.

Click and drag the top of the Activity Feed panels to customize your Stream Manager layout.

Now, Activity Feed supports common third-party events from tools such as Streamlabs, StreamElements, and more! Learn more here.

My Chat

Monitor and interact with Chat during your stream. Click the 3 Horizontal Dots in the top right-hand corner of the panel to see the Users in Chat or to enable Popout Mode for Chat. You can also adjust your Chat Settings (such as changing your Chat mode to Emotes-Only Chat) by clicking the Cog in the bottom right of the panel.

Stream Preview

See how your stream appears on your channel. Click the 3 Horizontal Dots in the top right-hand corner of the panel to hide the video player or to enable Popout Mode.

Stream Stats

Monitor the length of your current stream session, as well as the number of viewers, views, followers, and your bitrate. You can customize which stats appear on your Stream Manager.

We are removing channel page views (or “Views”) from Stream Manager Stats on April 14, 2022. The data tells an incomplete story which can be confusing and misleading to creators. Here’s why: your total “Views” only includes channel page loads on desktop web, and is not inclusive of mobile or other viewing surfaces - so it’s not a true representation of your live audience and engaged community.

Metrics that are more accurate indicators of your channel growth and community engagement include: average viewers, minutes watched, follows, and unique chatters. You can select these stats from the arrows in your Channel Analytics:

To learn more about the analytics that are currently available in your dashboard, visit the Channel Analytics help article. To leave feedback on analytics improvements, visit UserVoice.

Quick Actions

Perform different actions at the click of a button. Customize your channel to easily access the Quick Actions that matter most when you’re live, including Raid a Channel, Clip That, Add Stream Marker, Start Watch Party and more. When you resize the Quick Actions panel the icons will adaptively adjust in size. You can also easily search for a specific Quick Action with the search bar, browse Quick Actions by category, or see recently released Quick Actions in the New Quick Actions section.

Edit Stream Info

Easily edit the title of your stream, your go live notification, your streaming category, tags, and stream language in this panel.

Mod Actions

Track actions taken by your Moderators such as timing out users, deleting messages, and changing Chat modes. Raids are also shown here. To filter out actions that are shown in this panel, click the 3 Horizontal Dots in the top right-hand corner of the panel and click the toggle next to the relevant alert.

Active Mods

Review Mods with an active connection to Chat.

Automod Queue

If your channel has AutoMod enabled, any messages held by AutoMod for review will appear here. Click the 3 Horizontal Dots in the top right-hand corner for options to clear the panel of messages, review Blocked/Permitted terms, and access AutoMod’s settings.

Rewards Request Queue

Twitch Affiliates and Partners can use this panel to manage their queue of custom rewards requested via Channel Points.

Visit the Channel Points Guide for more info on setting up and managing Channel Points.

Stream Health

See live data about your bitrate and FPS. You can also click the link at the bottom of the panel to view additional details in the Twitch Inspector page.

Hosting You

See which creators are currently hosting your channel.

Unban Requests

View and manage unban requests from banned chatters here. Unban requests can be sorted using the drop-down menu. If you choose to deny an unban request, that user will not be able to submit another request.

Predictions

Twitch Affiliates and Partners can use this panel to set an event and its possible outcomes and let viewers use Channel Points to predict the end result before the prediction window closes. Viewers who guess correctly will win a proportionate share of the Channel Points pool. See Channel Points Predictions for more info on setting up and managing Predictions.

Stream Summary Analytics

The Stream Summary page in your Creator Dashboard shows you data for individual streams, so you can analyze your most recent stream, or revisit previous streams to compare how you performed stream over stream. For a snapshot of how your channel is doing overall, visit the Overview page.

Got questions on experiments? See below

What’s in a Stream Summary?

Your Stream Summary will contain the following information:

Key Stats

See key data about your most recent stream, such as viewers, followers, chatters, and compare your performance to the previous stream.

Viewer Engagement Panel

This panel shows viewer engagement metrics to help you understand all the ways your viewers interacted throughout the stream so you can spot opportunities to create more engaging moments.

  • View which moments in your stream netted you the most follows and subs, when clips were created, when viewers peaked, and much more.
  • VODs under 2 hours long will be narrowed down to 1-minute increments. Longer VODs will have the following granularity:
    • VODs between 2-4 hours: 2-minute increments
    • VODs between 4-10 hours: 5-minute increments
    • VODs between 10-24 hours: 20-minute increments
  • For stream sessions with multiple VODs, you can select which VOD you wish to see viewer engagement for.
Emote Performance

See the usage of your emotes across Twitch. Learn more about emote analytics or see your own.

Top Clips From This Stream

Easily view and identify your most viewed clips from this stream. Scroll through up to 5 of your most viewed clips and easily export your favorite moments directly to your social accounts like TikTok and YouTube. Clips from your stream are also added to your Stream Recap, so viewers can catch up on what they missed.

If there’s a duplicate clip of the same stream moment, we will only surface the clip with more views.

We know that sharing your highlights from a stream quickly can make a big difference in audience engagement. While views aren’t always a perfect indicator of a share-worthy clip, we hope this feature streamlines your workflow after a stream to help you identify potential top clips and share them directly to your networks in one place.

Clip views peak the first few days, so make sure to check back often. This feature is also available in the mobile app.

How Viewers Found Your Stream

See a detailed breakdown of what sources your viewers came to your stream from.

Go Live Notification Data

The number of people that engaged with go live notifications sent out for streams in the selected data range. This shows the amount of engagement (# followers who clicked or tapped on your go live notification) and your notification reach (# of followers who have notifications for your channels enabled). See your stats here.

Switching between stream summaries is as simple as clicking the arrows or date / stream number at the top of the summary, you will then be prompted to select an available summary.

Experiments

A limited amount of creators will have access to experimental features within their Stream Summary!

Frequently Asked Questions

How soon after my stream will my Stream Summary data be available?
Your Stream Summary data will be updated within 15 minutes of your stream ending. To make sure you don’t miss out on a single Stream Summary, opt in to receiving the Stream Summary email by visiting your Notifications Settings, selecting By Email, and toggling on Stream Stats updates. You will only receive an email after streams that are more than 30 minutes long and have at least one viewer.
How far back in time can I see data in the Viewer Engagement panel?
Viewer Engagement panel data for your VOD is accessible for 30 days from the stream date, as long VOD storage is enabled. VOD storage for Affiliates is 14 days. VOD storage for Partners and Turbo/Prime users is 60 days.
Where can I leave feedback about Stream Summary?
You can leave feedback on Stream Summary by clicking the ? button on the top right of the page and selecting Send Feedback. Alternatively, would love to hear your feedback here, especially if you have any thoughts around stats, or panels that we should include.
How is Stream Summary different from the rest of my Analytics?
Stream Summary is a quick overview of one stream. When you want to dive deeper or compare performance across different time periods, jump over to the other pages in Analytics.
How do I view my Stream Summary from previous streams?
Click the left and right arrows next to the date at the top of your Stream Summary page to navigate between streams. We only save your last 30 Stream Summaries, but you can always visit your Analytics page for insights from older streams.
Is Stream Summary available on mobile?
Yes.
I would prefer not to always see my stats. Is there a way I can hide them from my Stream Summary?
You can’t hide stats in the Stream Summary right now. We understand that you’re more than just the raw numbers of your stream; check out your achievements.
Why don’t I see Top Clips from This Stream?
If you don’t see this panel in your Stream Summary, that means there were no clips created of that stream.

Streaming From Your Browser (Beta)

Go live on Twitch directly from your browser, with no software to download and no complicated setup.

Anyone can stream from their browser, but we recommend it especially if your setup is just you, a camera, a microphone, and optionally, a shared screen. Our browser streaming interface works great for new streamers and simple, talk-first streams like IRL (“In Real Life”) and Just Chatting. This guide walks you through your first stream from start to finish, so you know what to expect at each step.

This feature is in beta and is available to a limited group of creators. If you don’t see Stream in your Creator Dashboard yet, you’re not in the beta.

Before You Start

Can’t find a setting this guide mentions? Type its name into Dashboard Search in your Creator Dashboard!

This guide assumes you have a Twitch account and a computer with a camera and microphone. You’ll also need a recent version of Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge for the best experience.

Going live from your browser works on a computer (desktop or laptop) only. To go live from your phone or tablet, use the Twitch mobile app instead. See Mobile IRL Broadcasting.

You should also have an idea for your stream. You don’t need a big plan, but knowing what you’ll talk about or show on stream makes being live much easier.

You should also be prepared to make a good first impression! New viewers often check your channel before they follow. Add a profile picture and a short bio to your Twitch account so they know who you are. See Channel Page Setup. If you already have followers on another platform, let them know where to find you on Twitch.

Browser streaming works best when you’re interacting live, on camera and talking. What you can do on stream depends on your equipment, but a webcam and microphone are enough to start.

Browser streaming offers a simpler way to go live, and it works best for streams that don’t need advanced features. Our browser streaming interface may not be the right choice:

  • If you’re trying to stream from a game console, like a PlayStation or Xbox, through your computer. That usually takes a capture card, a device that brings the picture from your console into your computer. You can also go live right from your console. See PlayStation Broadcasting and Xbox Broadcasting.
  • If you’re trying to bring custom designs on your stream, like your own frames around your camera, animated graphics, or on-screen widgets that show things like donations or a countdown. Browser streaming includes simple scenes and alerts instead.
  • If you use several cameras, mics, or other sources at once, or lots of scenes you switch between.

For streams that meet these characteristics, see Ready for More?

Stay Safe and Know the Rules

Twitch is built to be a welcoming place for everyone, and keeping it safe is a shared responsibility. Make sure to familiarize yourself with the Twitch Community Guidelines, our rules on what is and isn’t allowed on Twitch. If you’ve streamed or posted on another platform, some of these may be different from what you’re used to, so take a few minutes to read them before your first stream.

Protect your privacy. Everything (yes, everything!) your camera and screen share capture is broadcast live. Sharing your location or personal info, like your address, phone number, or email, can be risky. Respect the safety, privacy, and property of others, including people who appear on your stream or are near you while you’re live.

Label your stream. If your stream includes mature topics, add the right Content Classification Labels when editing stream info, so viewers know what to expect.

Set up moderation before you go live. Turn on AutoMod and consider asking a trusted friend to be a moderator. To find these settings, search for “AutoMod” or “Roles Manager” in Dashboard Search. If chat gets out of hand, Shield Mode lets you lock things down quickly. Learn more: Setting Up Moderation for Your Twitch Channel.

Protect your account. Turn on Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) to help keep your account secure. You’ll find it in Security and Privacy settings.

Set Up Your Stream

The first time you go live in our browser interface, we walk you through a few steps:

  • In your Creator Dashboard, select Stream.
  • (First time only) On the Go live on Twitch from your browser page, select Set up stream.
  • Your browser asks to use your camera and microphone, so Twitch can show and hear you on stream. Select Allow.
  • Pick the alerts pack you want to use, so new follows and subscriptions are celebrated on your stream automatically. If you’ve already set up alerts, you’ll still pick a pack here, so choose the one you want viewers to see. You can change how they look later in Alerts in your Creator Dashboard.
  • Select See Stream Layout to open your layout.

If you’ve already explored the browser interface, this stream layout page is where you’ll set up your stream each time you go live. You may need to fix any permission errors before proceeding. You can go there directly at dashboard.twitch.tv/stream. Or, on twitch.tv, select your profile picture, then Start Streaming.

Your Stream Layout

Your stream layout is what viewers see: your camera, plus boxes for alerts and chat. For example, you might show your camera full screen with chat in one corner. Nothing in your layout is visible to viewers until you go live.

Preview and Scenes

Preview shows your stream as viewers will see it. Drag the Alerts and Chat boxes to move them.

The chat messages in Preview are samples that show where chat will appear. They aren’t from real viewers. Send a message in your Stream Chat to see a real message pop up.

Scene Presets are 3 ready-made scenes you can switch between before and during your stream: Starting Soon is a holding screen before you go live. Hold on Starting Soon for a few minutes while your audience shows up, but don’t wait too long! Main Scene is your main scene while streaming. Select it when you’re ready to be on camera. Finally, Be Right Back lets you step away without ending your stream.

Make Starting Soon and Be Right Back your own in Scene Customization. Pick a Background or select Add Background to upload your own (PNG, JPEG, or WEBP up to 25 MB; GIF, MP4, or WEBM up to 100 MB), then add an Image asset and a Title.

Camera, Mic, and Screen Share

Use the stream controls to turn your camera and mic on or off, share your screen, and show or hide chat and alerts on your stream. In your mic settings, you can test your mic and hear yourself.

To share your screen, choose a browser tab, a window, or your entire screen, like you would on a video call.

Want viewers to hear what you share? Sound from your screen share, like music or a video, only reaches your stream if audio sharing is turned on. What happens depends on what you share:

  • A browser tab: Tab audio is shared by default. Before you confirm, check that the option to share tab audio is still on.
  • A window or your entire screen: Audio sharing is off by default. Turn on the option to share audio in your browser’s sharing window before you confirm. Some browsers and computers can’t share audio from a window or screen. If you don’t see the option, share a browser tab instead.

Test your sound before you go live, so you don’t find out mid-stream that viewers can’t hear it.

You’re responsible for everything you show on stream. Viewers see whatever you share, including notifications, messages, and open tabs. Sharing a single tab or window instead of your entire screen helps keep personal info private.

Edit Stream Info

Select the pencil next to your stream title, or open Quick Actions and select Edit Stream Info.

Add a title, a category, and tags so the right viewers can find you, and check Content Classification Labels if your stream includes mature topics. You’ll see other settings too, but you don’t need to change most of them for your first stream.

Quick Actions allow you to take useful actions during your stream. By default, they include Twitch, Clip That, Raid Channel, and Manage Goals. See Your First Stream for ways to use them.

Live Activity and Chat

See new followers and other activity in Live Activity, and talk with viewers in Stream Chat, on the same page. Live Activity may also show cards about other Twitch features. You can come back to them later, or close them to keep your feed clear.

Your First Stream

Before you go live, take a minute to check:

  • You can see yourself in Preview, and your mic test sounds right.
  • If you’re sharing sound from your screen, audio sharing is turned on.
  • Your title and category describe your stream.
  • AutoMod is on, and you know how to turn on Shield Mode.
  • Nothing personal is on camera, and anything you don’t want viewers to see is closed.

When you’re ready, select Go Live. Starting on Starting Soon gives you a moment to settle in. Switch to Main Scene when you’re ready to start.

If you open or switch to another tab, your stream keeps running, and a Picture-in-Picture popout may appear so you can keep an eye on it. You can return to your streaming tab at any time.

Don’t refresh or leave your streaming tab. If you refresh the tab, close it, or go to another page in that same tab, your stream ends.

What to Expect While You’re Live

Small streams are normal. It’s common to start with only a few viewers, or none. Keep talking as if someone is there, so your stream feels welcoming when viewers arrive.

When someone chats for the first time, Twitch highlights their message so you can welcome them (see First-Time Chatter Highlight). When someone follows you, an alert plays on your stream. If you’re an Affiliate or Partner, viewers can also subscribe and Cheer with Bits.

Another streamer can raid you, ending their stream by sending their viewers to you. A raid can bring a lot of new people at once, so it’s a good moment to say hello. If a raid doesn’t feel right, Shield Mode can help. See How to Use Raids.

Need a break? Switch to Be Right Back. Your stream keeps going if the tab is in the background, but leaving the page or closing the tab ends your stream, so you’ll be asked to confirm first.

Use Twitch, Clip That to save a fun moment you can share later and share it where your followers already are, like other social platforms (see How to Create, Edit, and Share Clips), or Manage Goals to set a follower goal your community can help you reach (see Community Goals). Before you end, use Raid Channel to send your viewers to a friend or a streamer you like. It’s a great way to make connections.

When you’re done, select End Stream.

If Something’s Not Right

Camera or mic blocked? Select the camera or lock icon in your browser’s address bar to allow access.

Connection dropped? Twitch tries to reconnect automatically. If it can’t, select Restart broadcast. To check your connection, see Guide to Broadcast Health.

After Your Stream

Your Stream Summary shows your viewers, new followers, and chat activity, usually within 15 minutes of your stream ending. To find it, search for “Stream Summary” in Dashboard Search. Turn on Stream Summary emails so you get it every time.

Plan your next stream. Add a stream schedule to your channel so viewers know when to come back (search for “Schedule” in Dashboard Search), and set up Go Live notifications so followers hear when you start.

Working toward Affiliate? As you keep streaming, you can work toward the Affiliate Program, which lets you earn from your stream. See Joining the Affiliate Program.

Ready for More?

When you want custom overlays, a capture card, or more scenes and sources, it’s time to move up to broadcasting software like OBS. See Recommended Software for Broadcasting and the How Do I Stream FAQ. To upgrade your camera or mic, see Recommended Hardware for Broadcasting.

Want to stream on the go? You can also go live from your phone with the Twitch mobile app. See Mobile IRL Broadcasting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this replacing OBS?
No. OBS and other broadcasting software are still great options when you want more control over your stream. Streaming from your browser is a simpler way to start, especially if you’re new to streaming.
Why don’t I see Stream in my Creator Dashboard?
This feature is in a limited beta, so not every creator has it yet. We don’t have a date to share for wider availability.

Transcoding Options FAQ

When you start a stream, Twitch may transform your broadcast into multiple quality formats so viewers can choose the option that works best for their device and network connection. These quality options are called transcodes.

There are multiple ways your viewers can get quality options on your stream:

  • Standard transcodes — Twitch creates quality variants of your stream server-side (or, via our servers). Partners receive standard transcodes on all broadcasts. Non-partnered channels receive standard transcodes based on availability.
  • Enhanced Broadcasting (Multiple Encodes) — Your broadcast software uses your GPU to send multiple quality variants directly to Twitch. Available to anyone using compatible software.
  • Dual Format and 2K streams using Enhanced Broadcasting and Server Side Transcode Support — Streams using Dual Format or 2k Enhanced Broadcasting receive added server-side transcode support, reducing encoding strain on your system. Available to Partners and select Affiliates. Read more about what added server-side transcode support means for these types of streams.

A stable internet connection is the most important factor in delivering a high-quality stream. Enhanced Broadcasting and transcodes supplement the viewing experience by offering additional quality variants, but they are not a substitute for a reliable network.

If quality options are available for a stream, viewers can access them via the Settings icon on the video player.

How Quality Options Work

Not everyone has the bandwidth to watch a high-quality 1080p60 broadcast, and network conditions can change over time. Quality options let your viewers lower the resolution to reduce buffering, or conserve data.

Quality options can come from different sources depending on how you stream:

Source

How it works

Who gets it

Standard Transcodes

Twitch creates quality variants from your stream on Twitch servers

Partners: always. Non-partners: when resources are available

Enhanced Broadcasting (Multiple Encodes)

Your broadcast software sends multiple quality variants directly (see guide for details)

Anyone using compatible broadcast software (see guide for details)

Dual Format or 2K Streams with Enhanced Broadcasting (Added Transcode support)

Dual Format and 2k (1440p) streams use Enhanced Broadcasting, which encodes multiple quality variants from your broadcast software. To reduce strain on your system and improve performance, Twitch also provides added server-side transcode support for Dual Format and 2K streams for Partners and select Affiliates. This added server-side transcode support still requires Enhanced Broadcasting but lets us utilize your GPU to encode the highest-resolution horizontal and vertical streams, while using server-side transcoding to fill in all the lower resolutions. Ultimately, this results in your viewers getting a higher-quality experience across all formats.

Partners and select Affiliates streaming in Dual Format or using 2K. Enhanced Broadcasting is still required for all Dual Format and 2K streams. Check your Advanced Broadcast Settings on the Stream Settings page in your Creator Dashboard to see if you have access.

Standard Transcode Availability

Standard transcoding requires computational resources on Twitch servers. These resources are limited. Twitch provides standard transcodes as follows:

  • Partners receive transcodes on every broadcast (first-priority access).
  • Non-partners (Affiliates and all other streamers) receive transcodes based on resource availability each time they go live.

Standard transcode availability is not influenced by follower count, viewer count, or past enforcement actions. It is determined by server resource availability at the time your stream starts.

Learn more about the Twitch Partner Program.

Enhanced Broadcasting, Dual Format, and 2k Streaming

If you want to provide your viewers with consistent quality options without relying on standard transcode availability, you can use Enhanced Broadcasting. Enhanced Broadcasting uses your GPU to create multiple quality variants directly from your broadcast software.

Regular Streams using Enhanced Broadcasting (Multiple Encodes)

With Enhanced Broadcasting, your broadcast software sends multiple quality variants directly from your computer. This means your viewers always have quality options available, regardless of standard transcode availability. Enhanced Broadcasting is available to all streamers on Twitch. Visit our guide for requirements and details.

Dual Format and 2K Streams using Enhanced Broadcasting

Dual Format or 2k (1440p) streams use Enhanced Broadcasting, which encodes multiple quality variants from your broadcast software. To reduce strain on your system and improve performance, Twitch also provides added server-side transcode support for these streams for Partners and select Affiliates. This added server-side transcode support lets us utilize your GPU to encode the highest-resolution horizontal and vertical streams, while using server-side transcoding to fill in all the lower resolutions. Ultimately, this results in your viewers getting a higher-quality experience across all formats. Check your Advanced Broadcast Settings on the Stream Settings page in your Creator Dashboard to see if you have access to added server-side transcode support for Dual Format and 2k streams.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why doesn’t my stream have quality options?

If you are not using Enhanced Broadcasting, your quality options depend on standard transcode availability. Standard transcodes are provided to Partners on every broadcast. For non-partners, standard transcodes are available as server resources allow.

To get consistent quality options, use Enhanced Broadcasting on any stream. You can also stream in Dual Format or 2K, which use Enhanced Broadcasting and also provide added server-side transcode support for Partners and select Affiliates.

I used to have quality options. Why don’t I any longer?
Standard transcode availability is determined each time your stream goes live based on server resource availability at that moment. Twitch does not remove transcoding options as an enforcement action or otherwise. If you want guaranteed quality options, use Enhanced Broadcasting, or stream in Dual Format or 2K.
Can I request quality options?

Standard transcodes are not available by request. However, you can provide your viewers with consistent quality options by using Enhanced Broadcasting, which sends multiple qualities from your broadcast software. If you stream in Dual Format or 2K with Enhanced Broadcasting, Partners and select Affiliates also receive added server-side transcode support.

Do not trust third-party services or websites that promise to transcode video after the broadcast is sent to Twitch.

What is the difference between transcodes and Enhanced Broadcasting encodes?

Standard transcodes are created by Twitch servers after your stream is received. They require server resources and are allocated based on availability (Partners get priority).

Enhanced Broadcasting encodes are created by your own broadcast software before the stream reaches Twitch. Because they come from your hardware, they are always available when Enhanced Broadcasting is enabled, with no server allocation needed.

Learn more: Enhanced Broadcasting With Multiple Encodes.

What is added server-side transcode support?

Dual Format and 2K streams use Enhanced Broadcasting, which encodes multiple quality variants from your broadcast software. To reduce strain on your system and improve performance, Twitch also provides added server-side transcode support for these streams for Partners and select Affiliates. This added server-side transcode support lets us utilize your GPU to encode the highest-resolution horizontal and vertical streams, while using server-side transcoding to fill in all the lower resolutions. Ultimately, this results in your viewers getting a higher-quality experience across all formats.

Check your Advanced Broadcast Settings on the Stream Settings page in your Creator Dashboard to see if you have access to added server-side transcode support for Dual Format and 2k streams.

How will I know if I qualify for added server-side transcode support?

All Partners and select Affiliates will qualify for additional transcode support for Dual Format and 2k Streams. Check your Advanced Broadcast Settings on the Stream Settings page in your Creator Dashboard to see if you have access to added server-side transcode support for Dual Format streams.

Please note that this added server-side transcode support is specific to Dual Format and 2k streams that use Enhanced Broadcasting and is entirely separate from transcode support for any other regular stream. Read more about transcode support for regular streams above.

Why can’t everyone have added server-side transcode support for Dual Format and 2K?
These resources are limited. We do our best to provide added server-side transcode support to as many Dual Format and 2K streams as possible. However, not every stream on Twitch will have this added support, and we can only guarantee it for Partners at this time. Check your eligibility status in your Stream Settings.
If I qualify, will I have added transcode support on every stream?

Yes, if you qualify for transcode support, you will have the added server-side transcode support on every 2K and/or Dual Format Enhanced Broadcasting stream. It will not be available for regular non-enhanced-broadcasting streams or Enhanced Broadcasting streams that are not in 2K or Dual Format. For those streams, your standard transcode support will apply. Read more about transcode support for regular streams above.

Please note: Twitch may stop providing added transcode support for your 2K or Dual Format streams for select reasons, such as if you are inactive for long periods of time or lose Partner or Affiliate status. You can always check your access to added transcode support for Dual Format and 2K streams in your Stream Settings.

Do I need to be a Partner to get quality options?

No. While Partner status guarantees standard transcodes on every broadcast, you can provide quality options to your viewers by using Enhanced Broadcasting with compatible broadcast software. Enhanced Broadcasting sends multiple quality variants directly from your computer, so your viewers always have options.

Additionally, if you stream in Dual Format or 2K with Enhanced Broadcasting, Partners and select Affiliates receive added server-side transcode support to further reduce system strain.

I have added transcode support but still experienced performance issues. What should I do?
  • Double check your qualification by visiting your Advanced Broadcast Settings on the Stream Settings page in your Creator Dashboard.
  • Some performance issues may not be related to Enhanced Broadcasting, Dual Format, or 2k and may be caused by temporary issues with your network provider.
Other streams have lower followers or viewers than me, and they have transcodes. Why don’t I?
Standard transcode availability is based on server resources at the time a stream starts — it is not influenced by follower count, viewer count, or channel size. Those streamers may be using Enhanced Broadcasting, or streaming in Dual Format or 2K, which provide quality options independently of standard transcode allocation.
How are my viewers impacted by quality options?

Viewers using mobile data can lower the video quality or switch to audio-only to conserve data.

Viewers with poor network connectivity can adjust stream quality to reduce buffering.

Without quality options, viewers must watch at whatever quality you broadcast. If their connection cannot support that quality, they may experience buffering. See our playback troubleshooting guide for tips viewers can use to resolve common issues.

Can I limit the quality options viewers see?
No. When quality options are available, all generated options are visible to viewers.
Do I need quality options to have a successful stream?
No. For best results without transcodes, send broadcasts to Twitch using our recommended broadcast settings. Twitch offers many tools and benchmarks for growth that are not tied to transcode availability.
How can I grow my stream without consistent transcode options?
Ensure that you are sending us a broadcast using the best encoding settings so that your stream is as stable as possible for as many people as possible by viewing our broadcast guidelines. Twitch offers many tools and benchmarks for growth that are not tied to the availability of transcodes. Visit Creator Camp for more resources on growing your stream.
I have not had quality options for a long time. When will I have quality options?
There are no workarounds to receive standard transcoding options. For non-partners, standard transcoding options are available as resources allow. However, you can provide your viewers with consistent quality options by using Enhanced Broadcasting, or by streaming in Dual Format or 2K.
Do past account enforcement actions influence transcode availability?
No. Past enforcement actions such as account suspensions or DMCA strikes do not influence transcode availability for Partners or non-partners.
Do Dual Format and 2K streams always require Enhanced Broadcasting?
Yes. Dual Format and 2K streaming always requires using Enhanced Broadcasting, even if you have added server-side transcode support.
A member of my community is having trouble viewing my stream. What can I do?

As a first step, make sure you’re broadcasting using our recommended settings. If you’ve done this, know that many factors can impact someone’s ability to view your stream — in most cases, it is likely not just your stream that is the source of their viewing problem.

You can direct your viewer to our playback troubleshooting guide for steps they can take on their end to resolve common viewing issues.

Twitch’s Alerts

Alerts are a great way to personalize and hype up events in your stream, from thanking a viewer for showing their support by subscribing to welcoming a new follower to your channel. They highlight your communities’ actions driving awareness of what happened and who did it while helping you forge a stronger bond with your viewers. Activating and customizing alerts help you communicate your unique brand, stand out from the pack, and build a deeper relationship with your audience.
