Twitch’s Alerts FAQ

Providing Feedback

We really want to hear your thoughts on Twitch’s Alerts. Whether there are things you like, things you dislike, or features you wish you had, we want to know about it!

You can share feedback directly with our product teams in the Alerts UserVoice.

Frequently Asked Questions

I made my alerts but they’re not appearing in my stream. Why aren’t they showing?
The most common reason is that you may not have copied over your browser source, which you can copy from each alert set. Once copied, add this URL to your broadcasting software as a new browser source to enable. You can test to see if it’s working by clicking Send Test Alert in the editing view.
Which broadcasting software can I use with these alerts?
You can use Twitch’s Alerts with any broadcasting software that supports browser sources, such as OBS or XSplit. Copy the browser source URL from your alert set in Creator Dashboard, then add it to your broadcasting software as a new browser source.
Can I use these alerts when broadcasting through the Twitch iOS and Android apps?
Yes. Twitch’s Alerts appear on your stream when you go live with your camera (IRL streaming) from the Twitch iOS and Android apps.
I have a suggestion/feedback; how can I get it to you guys?
We’d love to hear it. So please head to our UserVoice and let us know your suggestions and feedback!
I received a notice that the audio I tried to upload was blocked because copyrighted material was identified in it. What does this mean?
Twitch values the work of songwriters, musicians, and other creative artists, and has developed a system to try and ensure that our community uses sounds that they own or have the right to use. If your upload was blocked and you received this notice, it means our system detected someone’s copyrighted audio in the file you selected. If you believe you received this message in error – for example, because you believe our system mistakenly identified copyrighted audio or you have the rights to upload and include the identified copyrighted audio in your streams and archives – please let us know via UserVoice.

Settings Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use multiple alert sets at once?
Yes! In fact, many streamers prefer to use multiple sets. The most common reason is because you may want to have an alert set for a specific game or holiday, which you can turn off from your Creator Dashboard when you don’t want to use them. Another reason to have multiple sets is if you want one type of alerts to show on a different part of the screen from another (e.g. have sub alerts in one spot and follower alerts in another) which you would add as separate browser sources.

Alert set off

Alert set on

What are some of the message variables?
Some variables will only work for specific events or will show differently depending on the type of alert and variation.

Variable

Description

{username}

Twitch name of the viewer who subscribed, gifted, cheered, followed, etc.

{tenure}

How long the subscriber has been subscribed to your channel.

{sub_tier}

The subscription tier the subscriber is subscribed to your channel at.

{amount}

The number of Bits, community-gifted subscriptions, or viewers joining with a raid.

{total_gifts}

The total number of subs the viewer has gifted.

{sender}

The Twitch name of the viewer who gifted a sub or community-gifted subs, unless they gifted anonymously.

For more variables check out our Types of Twitch’s Alerts article.

What are the file size limits for the alert images and sounds?
We support static image sizes up to 25MB and video sizes up to 100MB. We support audio file sizes up to 25MB.
How do I set up my alerts in XSplit?
We recommend setting up your Twitch’s Alerts browser source as a linked source when you copy and paste it across multiple scenes in your XSplit presentation. If you don’t, you may hear multiple overlapping sounds for the same alert. For more details on XSplit linked sources, see XSplit Linked Sources.

Creator Frequently Asked Questions

I am not an Affiliate/Partner. But can I still use Twitch’s Alerts?
Yes! You can use Twitch’s Alerts for things like new followers and raids.

Third-Party Alerts Frequently Asked Questions

How can I suggest additional third-party alert support?
Visit us in UserVoice and let us know what additional third-party alert support you’d like to see!
What happens when I authorize a third-party service to access my Twitch account?
When you authorize a third-party app or service to use your Twitch account, you’re agreeing that Twitch may receive information and data from that third-party service on your behalf. If you no longer wish to connect your Twitch account with these third-party services, you can disconnect your account at any time here: twitch.tv/settings/connections
I am a developer, how can I get my alerts into Twitch’s Alerts?
We’d love to hear from you! Contact us using this form.

Bonus Animated Emote Slots With Alerts

Affiliates and Partners can unlock 2 additional Animated Emote by using Twitch’s Alerts. The emote slots are yours for 60 days, reset each time an alert triggers on your stream.

I’m using Twitch’s Alerts, but my bonus emotes aren’t showing up!
In order to access the bonus animated emote slots, one of Twitch’s Alerts needs to trigger on your broadcast. Be sure that one of the events you have set up have happened on your channel. Once they have occurred and triggered an Alert, it can take up to 48 hours for the slots to become available.
How does unlocking the bonus animated alert slots for 60 days work with Twitch’s Alerts?
Whenever one of Twitch’s Alerts goes off on your stream, you get access to the 2 T1 bonus slots for 60 days. The 60 days resets each time an alert triggers so if you are using Twitch’s Alerts consistently, you will have constant access to your bonus slots!
Can Affiliates also have additional slots in the T2/3 sub areas? We want to reward those who sub at those tiers too!
Thank you for this feedback! It’s been shared with the team and they are currently exploring this.

Understanding Viewer Count vs. Users in Chat

This article will help creators understand the difference between Viewer Count (number of people viewing now) vs. Users in Chat (number of current chat participants).

Wondering if muted streams count as a view or why your Users in Chat list may not match your Viewer Count? Visit our FAQ.

Viewer Count

The Viewer Count is the number of viewers watching your live video at one time. Any time someone watches live video they’ll be counted as a viewer, whether or not they have a Twitch account or are signed in. Once they stop watching the live video, that number will go down. When a viewer starts or stops watching live video, it can take up to a few minutes for the Viewer Count to reflect this.

Viewer Count is displayed in red on or below the video player on Twitch.

Users in Chat

Users in Chat are displayed by clicking the Community icon located at the top of Twitch chat. This is the list of people connected to your chat, and is counted separately from Viewer Count. This list only includes logged in Twitch users that have connected to your chat – including lurkers, anyone that has chat popped out of the video page, or in chat-only mode on mobile devices.

You can click the Collapse icon to close Chat and remove yourself from Users in Chat.

To access the Users in Chat list on mobile devices, tap the Viewer Count displayed on the video feed.

Viewer Count vs. Users in Chat

People who watch video without chat connected will be counted in Viewer Count, and not shown in Users in Chat, regardless of if they are logged in or out. Some 3rd party tools incorrectly show Users in Chat as a raw number and may refer to it by a different name, such as viewers or viewer list. Non-Twitch tools, such as 3rd party extensions, may not accurately report these values.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is my Viewer Count X when I know I have Y users in chat?
Viewer Count is the number of people viewing your video stream, whether or not they are logged into a Twitch account. Users in Chat is the list of logged-in Twitch accounts connected to your chat. Some users may connect to chat, but not watch live video – including bots, users in chat-only mode, or users in popout chat mode. As a result, this means your list of Users in Chat could be different from your Viewer Count.
Do chat bots count towards Viewer Count?
Chat bots do not count towards your viewer count, as they do not view your stream. Instead, chat bots that join your chat can be viewed in your Users in Chat list.
How often does Viewer Count update?
When users start or stop watching live video, it can take up to a few minutes for the Viewer Count to update.
How often does Users in Chat update?
When users close or Collapse chat, it can take up to a few minutes for Users in Chat to update.
Will I appear in the Users in Chat list if I have chat in popout mode, or if my mobile app is in chat-only mode?
Yes, so long as you are logged into your Twitch account. Users in Chat do not count towards Viewer Count unless they are watching live video on the same device.
Does a muted stream count as a view?
Yes! Whether you mute the video player on Twitch, or the browser tab, you still count as a viewer so long as live video is playing.
If I have a stream open playing live video in another tab, do I still count as a viewer?
Yes, if live video is playing, you will count as a viewer, even if that tab is not in focus.
What about if the stream is playing in the background on mobile?
Yes, if live audio is playing or if you have minimized the live stream in the background on mobile, you will count as a viewer.

Xbox Broadcasting

Xbox broadcasting is managed by Microsoft. For detailed setup instructions, troubleshooting, and technical support, visit Xbox Support.

SUPPORT SCOPE: Xbox broadcasting functionality is managed by Microsoft, not Twitch. Twitch Support cannot troubleshoot Xbox console streaming issues, Xbox OS updates, or Xbox hardware problems. Direct all Xbox broadcasting questions to Xbox Support at support.xbox.com

The Twitch App on Xbox is for viewing only. To broadcast to Twitch from your Xbox console, use the native Xbox streaming feature or cloud broadcasting services.

How to Broadcast From Your Xbox

To stream to Twitch from your Xbox console:

  • Press the Xbox Button on your controller
  • Navigate to Capture & Share
  • Select Live streaming and follow the prompts

For complete setup instructions, system requirements, and account linking help, visit Xbox Support’s streaming guide.

Cloud Broadcasting Services: You can also stream using Streamlabs or Lightstream. Contact those services directly for setup and support.

For general streaming guidance, see our How Do I Stream FAQ and Twitch Creator Camp.

Troubleshooting

Xbox broadcasting issues: For problems with Xbox console streaming, system updates, network connectivity, party chat, or hardware issues, contact Xbox Support.

Cloud broadcasting services: For issues with Streamlabs or Lightstream, contact those services directly.

Twitch stream key issues: If you need to reset your stream key, go to your Creator Dashboard > Preferences > Channel and click Reset. Only reset once to avoid a 15-minute lockout.

Co-Streaming on Twitch

Content in this article is intended for brands and Twitch Partners already approved to co-stream. Brands, businesses, or those seeking to allow co-streaming for their content may contact Twitch here. Learn more.

Features described in this article may not be available for all devices or on mobile.

What is Co-Streaming?

Co-Streaming is a Twitch feature designed to help Main Broadcasters amplify the reach of their live events by giving allowlisted streamers (Co-Streamers) permission to add their own content to the stream and rebroadcast that content, as well as the stream, to their own communities. Co-Streaming also provides the Main Broadcaster aggregated analytics across all approved Co-Streams, giving a complete and accurate view of their event’s total reach and impact across Twitch.

This feature is designed for special broadcasts with extra-large reach such as esports tournaments or major streamer-led shows. These examples highlight the kinds of events that work best for Co-Streaming:

  • Large-scale esports events broadcast worldwide
  • Official game announcements streamed to global audiences
  • Community-driven celebrations of content creators
  • Record-breaking events featuring influencer-led entertainment

Here are a few terms you’ll see often when talking about Co-Streaming:

  • Main Broadcaster: The channel actively broadcasting a special large-scale stream and enabling Twitch users to Co-Stream their content. This includes large event organizers, brands and select partners.
  • Co-Streamer: The streamer who has been allowlisted by the Main Broadcaster to Co-Stream the main broadcast to their audience.
  • Broadcast or main broadcast: The content, usually of a large-scale event or show, being broadcast live by the Main Broadcaster and Co-Streamed by streamers.
  • Co-Streaming: The act of rebroadcasting the Main Broadcaster stream while using the Co-Stream product.

Co-Streaming Guidelines

Guidelines for Main Broadcasters
  • Co-Streaming is designed for special broadcasts with extra-large reach such as esports tournaments or major streamer-led shows. Access to this feature may be revoked at any time if misused.
  • When you enable Co-Streaming, you allow Co-Streamers to stream and record VODs and Clips of your stream on their channels. If the Co-Streamers have turned on the Clips feature, you also allow their viewers to record Clips of your stream and share that content off Twitch. At this time, Co-Streaming is not supported for streamers enrolled in the DJ Program or for broadcasts in the DJs category,since the DJs category and DJ Program do not allow for VODs to be published. Learn more.
  • Twitch will not enforce your brand’s rules or guidelines on how you’d like Co-Streamers to engage with your broadcast. You are fully responsible for communicating and managing them. If a Co-Streamer violates Twitch’s Terms of Service or Community Guidelines (CG), you may file a user report.
  • You can manage who is authorized to Co-Stream your broadcast by updating your Allowlist. If someone outside your Allowlist Co-Streams your broadcast, you may file a DMCA notification in accordance with our DMCA Guidelines.
  • As a reminder, all Twitch users, including Main Broadcasters, are responsible for what they stream or upload to their channels and for complying with Twitch’s Community Guidelines and Terms of Service.
Guidelines for Co-Streamers
  • You are responsible for complying with Twitch’s Community Guidelines and Terms of Service when you stream or upload to your channel, including when you are Co-Streaming.
  • If the Main Broadcaster engages in behavior that violates Twitch’s Terms of Service or Community Guidelines, you will not be held responsible for that behavior so long as you clearly condemn it. However, Twitch may remove the main broadcast, which will also end your Co-Stream. We encourage all Co-Streamers to be mindful of the content they Co-Stream.
  • The Main Broadcaster is responsible for their broadcast, and you are responsible for choosing to Co-Stream it.
  • If a main broadcast contains unauthorized copyrighted material, both you and the Main Broadcaster could receive a DMCA notification from the rights holder. If the main broadcast is removed by Twitch, that will also end your Co-Stream.
  • To be recognized as an official Co-Streamer for the Main Broadcast, you must initiate the Co-Stream by clicking the “Co-Stream” button on the Main Broadcaster’s channel, even if you are already capturing the broadcast via third-party tools such as OBS. Simply rebroadcasting without initiating the Co-Stream on Twitch will prevent your viewership from counting toward the broadcast’s total reach, and will not allow the Main Broadcaster to see that you are streaming their broadcast as an allowlisted Co-Streamer.
  • By Co-Streaming, you acknowledge that Twitch ads appearing on the main broadcast will appear on your channel as part of the Co-Stream if you are not Subscribed to the channel you are co-streaming, or you do not have Twitch Turbo. Co-Streaming effectively streams the Main Broadcaster’s feed in real time, so all content, including ads, overlays, and other broadcast elements, will be visible to your audience. These ads do not count as ads on your channel, and your monetization is not affected.
  • Content Classification Labels from the Main Broadcaster’s stream will automatically be applied to your Co-Stream, unless you change them. Co-Streamers are responsible for setting the appropriate CCLs and branded content labels on their content, including during Co-Streams.
Potential Cases of Abuse or Misuse of Co-Streaming

The following behaviors are considered potential misuse or abuse of Co-Streaming. Using the Co-Streaming product in unintended ways may lead to suspension or removal of Co-Streaming privileges. Understanding these examples can help you stay within the intended use of the feature:

  • Violations of Twitch Policies
    • Main Broadcasters or allowlisted Streamers who engage in conduct during a Co-Stream that violates Twitch’s Terms of Service or Community Guidelines may face enforcement actions. This may include enforcement for the underlying violation.
  • Co-Streaming by Streamers Who Are Not Allowlisted
    • Any streamer not included on the Main Broadcaster’s Allowlist who attempts to re-broadcast a broadcast is doing so without authorization. Such streams may be subject to DMCA claims.
  • Abuse of Co-Streaming Privileges As a Main Broadcaster
    • Channels falsely presenting themselves as the Main Broadcaster to divert viewers away from the Main Broadcast.
    • Main Broadcasters re-broadcasting their own streams across multiple channels or alternate accounts, creating duplicate or disparate versions of the same content.
    • Using Co-Streaming on regular, non-event content purely for self-promotion and viewership tampering rather than its intended use for special broadcasts. Any behavior that manipulates or distorts viewership counts when Co-Streaming is strictly prohibited. For more details, please review Twitch’s Community Guidelines on Viewership Tampering.
How to Become a Main Broadcaster

Currently, this feature is designed for special broadcasts with extra-large reach such as esports tournaments or major streamer-led shows. This includes large event organizers, brands and select partners.

To get started, reach out to Twitch through your partnerships or support contact. Your contact can guide you through eligibility, setup, and best practices for maximizing your broadcast’s reach.

If you have an event that should be Co-Streamable but do not have a contact at Twitch please reach out to Twitch Support 24/7 via email at help.twitch.tv/s/contactsupport.

How to Begin Co-Streaming

Main Broadcaster
  • In web only, navigate to Stream Manager in order to set up your Co-Stream Settings
  • Under the Edit Stream Info Panel, you will find the Co-Streaming Section. There, you can edit your Allowlist, limit which user groups can Co-Stream your broadcast and enable the Co-Streaming setting
To Update your Allowlist:

  • Under the Co-Stream Section in the Edit Stream Info panel, click the “Edit” button next to My Allowlist

  • From there, you can add trusted streamers to your Co-Stream allowlist by searching for them in the search bar. These users will always be able to Co-Stream your content if you have Co-streaming enabled

  • Once finished, click “Done”. This will take you back to the Stream Manager page where you can see that your Allowlist has been updated.

  • Once Co-Streaming is turned on, you can notify allowlisted Co-Streamers when broadcast is set to start and that they may Co-Stream your broadcast.

You can choose to limit Co-Streaming to JUST your Allowlist or your Allowlist AND all Partners and Affiliates, under the Co-Stream settings.

To Enable Co-Streaming:
  • Once you are ready to enable Co-Streaming for your broadcast, toggle the “Enable Co-Streaming” button under the Co-Stream Section in the Edit Stream Info panel
  • Once the button is toggled, the broadcast analytics will begin to aggregate and reflect in the top panel. The analytics widgets will show you:
    • That you are actively Co-Streaming
    • How many viewers you have for your broadcast on your channel
    • How many total viewers you have for your broadcast across your channel and all Co-Streamers
    • How many streamers are actively Co-Streaming your broadcast
To Stop Co-Streaming:
  • When your broadcast has concluded and you are ready to stop the Co-Stream, toggle the “Enable Co-Streaming” button under the Co-Stream Section in the Edit Stream Info panel. This will disable the ability to Co-Stream your broadcast.

Please make sure your broadcast is over to ensure accurate viewership counting. Co-Streaming is intended to remain on for the duration of your broadcast. Disabling and re-enabling Co-Streaming creates separate broadcast segments and prevents Twitch from automatically aggregating analytics. To access complete analytics across all broadcast segments, you need to reach out to your Twitch account partner.

Accessing Co-Stream Analytics:
  • You can access your Co-Stream Analytics by going to your Creator Dashboard and navigating to Stream Summary under the Analytics tab.
  • Your Co-Stream analytics will appear under the Co-Stream section of your Stream Summary. Your Co-Stream analytics may take up to 4 hours to generate. We will send you a notification when your Co-Stream analytics are ready to view.
Co-Streamer
To begin Co-Streaming a Co-Streamable broadcast:

  • Ensure you start streaming the event through a third party tool like OBS or XSplit.

  • Once you have confirmed you are streaming the Main Broadcast, navigate to the Main Broadcast’s channel and click on the stream you wish to Co-Stream

  • You can verify that you are approved to Co-Stream the broadcast if you see a banner at the top of the stream indicating it.

  • To begin Co-Streaming, click on the Co-Stream button next to the Main Broadcaster’s name.

  • You will be prompted to confirm that you’d like to start Co-Streaming the broadcast.

To Stop Co-Streaming:
  • You can stop Co-Streaming the broadcast either by:
    • Clicking on the “Stop Co-Streaming” button from the Main Broadcaster’s stream
  • Going to your Stream Manager, and clicking on the “Stop Co-Streaming” button located in the top banner.

To be recognized as an official Co-Streamer for the Main Broadcast, you must initiate the Co-Stream by clicking the “Co-Stream” button on the Main Broadcaster’s channel, even if you are already capturing the broadcast via third-party tools such as OBS.

Frequently Asked Questions

What counts as a “Special Event” on Twitch?
Special Events are unique, one-time broadcasts that go beyond a streamer’s regular content. Examples include charity streams, esports tournaments, product announcements, subathons, and major influencer-led shows.
Why is Co-Streaming required for the combined viewership?
These products enable us to confirm that the collaboration is authentic and that the communities are truly engaging together in a co-op experience that meets the requirements for Shared Viewership. As we learn how these features affect streamers and viewers, we will look to use the same principles in enabling other collaboration products to facilitate Co-Streaming.
What does Total Event Viewership affect?
For Co-Streaming events, the Total Event Viewership (the combined viewership across all Co-Streams) is attributed to the Main Broadcast. It appears on the Main Broadcaster’s channel page and in followers’ Followed Channels list, and it determines where the Main Broadcast appears on followers’ Following page when they sort by Viewers (High to Low). It does not affect where the Main Broadcast appears when viewers browse a category and sort by viewer count. Categories use each channel’s own viewer count. Main Broadcasters also get enhanced analytics to understand the total reach of their broadcast, which can be valuable for sponsorships and other opportunities.
Won’t people game the system?
We understand the concern about potential misuse, which is why we are spending the time to clearly define the guidelines for what is permissible and restricting initial usage to both Co-Streaming and Shared Viewership. We will be actively enforcing our policies to retain trust in the feature.
What should Co-Streamers consider regarding risks of Terms of Service violations?
Co-Streamers are responsible for what they stream or upload to their channel, and must comply with Twitch’s Community Guidelines and Terms of Service at all times, including when they are Co-Streaming. All Co-Streamers should carefully review the Co-Streaming Guidelines outlined in this article.
As a brand, business, or Twitch Partner, how can I enable Co-Streaming for my stream?
Currently, this feature is designed for special broadcasts with extra-large reach such as esports tournaments or major streamer-led shows. This includes large event organizers, brands and partners.
To get started, reach out to Twitch through your partnerships or support contact. Your contact can guide you through eligibility, setup, and best practices for maximizing your broadcast’s reach.
If you have an event that should be Co-Streamable but do not have a contact at Twitch, you may contact us at this form. Please note, not all requests will receive a response.
Can I just rebroadcast the event without using Twitch’s Co-Streaming?
Only streamers who have been added to the Main Broadcaster’s Allowlist are authorized to Co-Stream. Any streamer not included on the Main Broadcaster’s Allowlist who attempts to re-broadcast a broadcast is doing so without authorization. Such streams may be subject to DMCA claims.
To be recognized as an official Co-Streamer for the Main Broadcast, you must initiate the Co-Stream by clicking the “Co-Stream” button on the Main Broadcaster’s channel, even if you are already capturing the broadcast via third-party tools such as OBS. Simply rebroadcasting without initiating the Co-Stream on Twitch will prevent your viewership from counting toward the broadcast’s total reach, and will not allow the Main Broadcaster to see that you are streaming their broadcast as an allowlisted Co-Streamer.
How does viewership work on my channel if I Co-Stream?
Your individual concurrent viewers (CCV) will still be counted for your own channel. At the same time, your audience will also be reflected in the Total Event Viewership, which measures the total reach across all Co-Streams of the event broadcast.
Will it affect Path to Partner or Ad payouts for Co-Streamers?
No, Co-Streaming does not affect Path to Partner or ad payouts for Co-Streamers. We want to first understand how creators utilize the tool before considering those implications.
As a streamer, why am I not able to Co-Stream a particular broadcast?
Co-Streaming is designed to help Main Broadcasters amplify the reach of their live events by giving allowlisted streamers (Co-Streamers) permission to add their own content to the stream and rebroadcast that content, as well as the stream, to their own communities. Main Broadcasters may restrict which channels are allowed to Co-Stream their content. If you attempt to rebroadcast a stream without being allowlisted by the Main Broadcaster, it is considered unauthorized and violates our Co-Streaming guidelines, and you may be subject to DMCA claims from the Main Broadcaster and/or Twitch enforcement.

Featured Clips

What are Featured Clips?

Featured Clips help you show up on new and existing Twitch discovery surfaces in ways that best represent you and your community – and no one knows how you’d like to be represented better than you!

Clips are a great way for new viewers to quickly discover streamers and get a feel for you and your community, even when you’re not live. With the addition of new tools like the mobile Discovery Feed, you have more control over which of your Clips are shown to viewers on Twitch.

Streamers and their editors can select Clips to be featured in the Discovery Feed and across Twitch. Streamers can also choose to grant featuring access to Moderators of their channel by visiting their Clips settings. There’s no limit to how many Clips you can feature, so feature any Clip that you think represents your community well. Twitch discovery surfaces prioritize recent and engaging Featured Clips, so featuring Clips after every stream will give you the best chance of being discovered.

Twitch discovery surfaces default to prioritizing Featured Clips ahead of non-Featured Clips, making Featured Clips one of your strongest discovery tools. Encourage your viewers, mods, and editors to create Clips of your channel and pick your favorite moments after each stream to help us promote your Clips to new viewers on Twitch!

Start taking advantage of the added discovery benefits today! Read more about how to feature Clips, who can feature Clips, and upcoming changes below.

Where Will Featured Clips Be Shown?

Featured Clips are prioritized ahead of non-Featured Clips for discovery across Twitch, giving you more control over which Clips are discoverable by viewers when you’re not live.

Who Can Feature Clips?

Streamers and their editors can feature any Clips of their channel created by any viewer on Twitch by default. Streamers can also grant featuring access to their Moderators by going to their Clips settings under Featured Clips > Permissions.

To edit or manage the roles of your community members, go to your Creator Dashboard. Click on the Community option in the menu, then Roles Manager. You will see a list of all the individuals who currently have a role (e.g., Editor, Moderator, VIP, and/or Artist) on your channel.

Please note: With this change to Clips, once a streamer, editor, or eligible Moderator features a Clip created by another viewer, the viewer will no longer be able to delete that Clip, or edit the Clip title. If the Clip is not featured, the viewer can still edit the title and delete the Clip.

How Do I Feature a Clip?

You can feature any Clips created of your channel, including past Clips. Today, streamers, their editors, and eligible Moderators can feature Clips in two ways:

  • Clips Manager
  • Clip Viewing Surfaces

We’re working on letting you feature Clips from additional surfaces, including your channel page, over time. Share your feedback and suggestions with us on UserVoice.

How to Feature Clips in your Clips Manager

The Clips Manager is a great place to feature your Clips because it allows you to feature several Clips at a time.

  • Use the checkboxes to the left of each Clip to select the ones you want to feature. You can batch select up to 20 Clips to feature at one time.
  • Once you’ve selected one or more Clips, choose Feature Selected and you’re done!

We’ve updated filters in the Clips Manager to make it easier for you to sort by your most recent, most viewed, and recommended Clips to quickly feature Clips from your existing inventory and after every stream.

  • On the “Clips of my Channel” tab in the Clips Manager, you can now filter by “All”, “Recommended”, and “Featured” Clips. You can also filter by when your Clips were created, from most recent (last 24 hours) to “All Time”. These filters mirror those on your channel page Clips tab.
  • We’ve also added these flows to the “Clips I’ve Created” tab to make it easier to feature Clips you’ve created from channels you have permission to feature on.
  • The default view will be your most recent “Recommended” Clips. At launch, a “recommended” Clip is one that a Clip curator has saved with a unique title. Clips with unique titles have been proven to drive better viewer outcomes and more views overall than those that do not have a unique title.

We recommend filtering to your most recent Clips and sorting by the most views to find Clips to feature from your current inventory and after every stream in the future!

How to Feature Clips when Viewing a Clip

When viewing a Clip of your own channel, or a channel that you are an editor of, click Feature this Clip below the video player. This applies to both twitch.tv and clips.twitch.tv

How Do I Unfeature a Clip?

You can unfeature Clips in the Clips Manager

  • Select the featured Clip(s) that you want to unfeature
    • You can view all of your Featured Clips easily by using the “Featured” filter.
    • Select only Clips that are currently featured. Once you have selected your Clip(s), an “Unfeature” button will appear at the top of the Clips Manager.

Featured Clips Analytics

We’ve added Featured Clips views to the Overview chart in your Analytics to help you get a sense of how Featured Clips are performing compared to non-featured Clips. Select “Clip Views” from the drop down navigation in the Overview chart to see your aggregate Featured Clips views compared to aggregate non-Featured Clips views within a set time frame.

Ever wondered how many clip views you’ve gotten from the Discovery Feed or Featured Clips shelves on the homepage? We’ve added new on-demand content analytics on the Discovery Analytics page to help you better understand where your Clip views are coming from. Click on the new “On-Demand Content” tab to see where viewers discovered your Clips, on and off Twitch. Select various sources to compare trends on the graph above.

Check out the My Channel Clips table below the on-demand metrics for more details on your most viewed Clips during a designated time period. Filter your clips by “All” or “Featured” and sort by Category and date to learn more about what types of Clips drive the most views. See a Clip with high views that you want to feature and prioritize in discovery? Go directly to the Clips Manager to select and feature the Clip.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will non-featured Clips still show up on Twitch?
Yes. Non-Featured Clips will still be shown in Twitch discovery surfaces.
Who is allowed to feature Clips?
Streamers and their editors can feature Clips by default. Streamers can choose to grant featuring access to Moderators by visiting their Clips settings. Moderators will be notified when they are given featuring permissions. Share your feedback and suggestions with us in UserVoice.
How do I add or remove an editor?
To manage the roles of your community members, go to your Creator Dashboard. Click on the Community option in the menu, then Roles Manager. You will see a list of all the individuals who currently have a role (e.g., Editor, Moderator, VIP, and/or Artist) on your channel.
How can Moderators feature clips?
Streamers can choose to grant featuring access to Moderators by visiting their Clips settings.
Do I have to feature my clips?
You are not required to feature your clips but not featuring your clips will limit your ability to get discovered on Twitch using Clips as we move towards a world of promoting exclusively Featured Clips.
Can I feature a Clip I made of another streamer?
No. Only streamers, their editors, and eligible Moderators can choose to feature Clips made of content on their channel.
Are Clip creators notified when I feature one of their Clips?
At launch, Clip creators will not be notified when their Clips are featured, but we’re working on adding this in the future.
Can I delete a Featured Clip?
Streamers, editors, and eligible Moderators can choose to unfeature a Featured Clip or delete the original clip of their channel entirely. Both actions can be taken in the Clips Manager. If you are a viewer that created a clip that was featured, the clip must be unfeatured before you can delete it.
Why can’t I delete a Clip I created after the streamer featured it?
With this change to Clips, once a streamer, editor, or eligible Moderator features a Clip created by another viewer, the viewer will no longer be able to delete that Clip. If the Clip is not featured, the viewer can still edit the title and delete the Clip.
How can I share feedback about Featured Clips?
Share feedback and suggestions about how we can improve Featured Clips in UserVoice.

Sub Codes

Codes (ex: xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx) received from third party partners can be redeemed on Twitch for Tokens at twitch.tv/redeem. Tokens can then be redeemed for a single month, Tier 1 subscription of your choice OR a Tier 1 gift subscription of your choice. Your specific code will come with a predetermined number of Tokens, geographic limitations, and expiration dates as noted on the third party partner website. Once a code has been redeemed for a Token, the Token(s) on your account have no expiration date.

Sub Tokens can be redeemed on web or mobile web. Sub Tokens cannot be redeemed in Twitch mobile apps.

If you have any questions about the details of your code such as when it expires or require additional assistance such as a replacement code, please reach out to the third party partner that distributed the Twitch code.

Sub Codes FAQ

What if I never got my Sub Code from the code distributor/third party?

Please reach out directly to the third party or responsible party for distributing codes. Twitch is unable to troubleshoot issues with codes distributed by a third party.

I am getting an error when I try to redeem the code, what should I do?

There’s a few reasons you might be getting an error. Your code may have expired, it may have already been redeemed, you may be entering the code incorrectly, or your specific geography (IP address) is not a valid location based on the terms set forth by the code distributor/third party. Please check with the third party guidelines on the code you received.

How do I know if my redemption was successful?

You should see a success message and you can check your Token balance by going to any channel page, opening the subscription window, and either selecting “Use my free sub” at the bottom of the screen OR selecting “Gift a Sub”. If you select “Use my free sub”, you should be shown a Sub Token option. If you select “Gift a Sub” you should see Sub Tokens as the only option for purchasing a Gift Subscription.

Tokens FAQ

How do I use a Token once I have it?

Navigate to any channel page to the channel’s subscription window or you can navigate to subs.twitch.tv/[Insert Channel Name]. Once you are in the subscription window, if you are using the Token on your own subscription, you can scroll to the bottom of the window and select “Use your free sub”, select “Sub Token” and then click “Subscribe with Sub Token.”

Sub Tokens can be redeemed on the web, or mobile web. Sub Tokens cannot be redeemed in the Twitch mobile app.

If you would like to redeem your Token for a Gift Subscription, navigate to “Gift a Sub” and your Token(s) will be automatically applied.

I am currently subscribed and would like to purchase gift subscriptions instead of using my Token(s), is this possible?

No, this is currently not possible. Your Token will be used first before you will be able to pay for a gift subscription.

How can I see how many Tokens I have available?

You can see your Tokens within the subscription window of any channel channel page by scrolling to the bottom and selecting “Use your free sub”

What if I don’t see the Token(s) I’ve redeemed or I can’t use them?

First, make sure that you aren’t attempting to redeem Token(s) in the Twitch mobile app. Tokens can be redeemed on the web, or mobile web. If you are still experiencing issues, please reach out to our support team by clicking the Contact Support link below.

Getting Started: Chat Functionality

About Content Pre-Approval

Whether you are a streamer or viewer, the Community Guidelines apply to everything you do on Twitch.

While it is natural for streamers to wonder if something they plan to do may violate Twitch’s Community Guidelines, Twitch cannot pre-approve any content or conduct in advance. As a result, we won’t be able to provide a yes/no answer if you contact Twitch Support with details seeking pre-approval on:

  • A planned stream
  • A planned emote, badge, or other user-created media
  • A planned channel trailer, profile or panel image, or other channel profile media
  • Any other conduct or content related to anything you do on Twitch

What You Can Do

As a first step, familiarize yourself with our Terms of Service and Community Guidelines. This is the best way to learn more about Safety on Twitch. Within the Community Guidelines, you can find specific examples and Enforcement Notes so you can better understand our rules and guidelines.

As a streamer, it is your responsibility to ensure your stream is a safe space promoting a positive experience for our global community. Our aim is to provide you with guidelines so you can feel confident fully expressing yourself within these boundaries.

Please note our support team is unable to provide guidance or pre-emptive evaluation on whether specific content meets our Community Guidelines or Terms of Service. We recommend erring on the side of caution if you are unsure.

If You Receive an Account Enforcement

When content is reported to us, we issue enforcements against accounts that we determine to have violated our Terms of Service or Community Guidelines. Learn more about this process, including how to appeal, in our guide About Account Enforcement and Chat Bans.

More Resources

  • Community Guidelines
  • Safety Center
  • Digital Millennium Copyright Act Notification Guidelines
  • Music Guidelines
  • Events Code of Conduct
  • Channel Points Acceptable Use Policy
  • Bits Acceptable Use Policy
  • Predictions Terms and Conditions

Chat Commands

Broadcasters and channel moderators appointed by the broadcaster are equipped with a set of commands and features that will allow them to closely monitor and moderate the chat. These features and commands range from giving a user a quick timeout to built in anti-spam.

To use any command or chat feature simply type the required command into the text-box and hit Enter.

Please note that…

  • words surrounded by curly brackets “{” and “}” symbols indicate a required value, for example: username would require a username (i.e. “Justin”).
  • A word surrounded by square brackets “[” and ”]” indicate an optional value, for example: seconds could optionally be left out, or replaced by a number of seconds (i.e. 10).
  • The symbols themselves ([, ], {, and }) are not to be included into the text box when entering your command.
  • Typing the forward slash (/) key will bring up a list of available commands.

Basic Commands for Everyone

Command

Description

/mods

This command will display a list of all chat moderators for that specific channel.

/gift quantity

Gift a specific number of Subs to the community

/vips

This command will display a list of VIPs for that specific channel.

/vote

Vote in the active poll in the given channel.

/color colorname

Allows you to change the color of your username. Normal users can choose between Blue, Coral, DodgerBlue, SpringGreen, YellowGreen, Green, OrangeRed, Red, GoldenRod, HotPink, CadetBlue, SeaGreen, Chocolate, BlueViolet, and Firebrick.

/color hex value

Turbo users can use the colors posted above as well as any Hex value (i.e: #000000).

/block username

This command will allow you to block all messages from a specific user in chat and whispers if you do not wish to see their comments.

In chat, users can also click on a username and then on the Block button on the user badge that appears.

In whispers, users can click on the cog icon at the top of the whisper window, and then on Block username.

You’ll be asked to provide one of three reasons for blocking the user.

/unblock username

This command will allow you to remove users from your block list that you previously added.

Users can also click on the Unignore button which replaces the Block button.

/disconnect

This command will simply disconnect you from the chat server. To reconnect, simply refresh the page.

/w username message

This command sends a private message to another user on Twitch.

@username

This command will allow you to target your message at a user, or reply directly to a specific message they’ve posted in the chat.

To Reply

This command will allow you to start a thread by replying directly to a message, or to add your message to an existing thread.

Windows

After using @username, press ALT + ENTER to enter reply mode.

When in reply mode, press ALT + UP or DOWN arrow keys to select a specific message to reply to.

Mac

After using @username, press ⌥ Options + ENTER to enter reply mode.

When in reply mode, press ⌥ Options + UP or DOWN arrow keys to select a specific message to reply to.

For more information about Chat Replies and how to use them, please see our help article.

Basic Commands for Broadcasters and all Moderators

Command

Description

/pin DESCRIPTION

Amplify high value chat messages for a longer duration in chat. You can also click the symbol directly in chat.

/shoutout username

This command allows you to share another streamer’s channel by showing a follow button in chat.

/announce description

Get chat’s attention by highlighting a message!

/monitor username

Start monitoring a user’s messages.

/unmonitor username

Stop monitoring a user’s messages.

/restrict username

Start restricting a user’s messages

/unrestrict username

Stop restricting a user’s messages

/user username

This command opens a user’s profile card where channel moderators and streamers can share channel-specific moderation comments, see when the user made their account, and view that user’s channel-specific chat, timeout, and ban history.

Can also be done by clicking the username in chat.

/timeout username seconds

This command allows you to temporarily ban someone from the chat room for 10 minutes by default. This will be indicated to yourself and the temporarily banned subject in chat on a successful temporary ban. A new timeout command will overwrite an old one.

The command also supports banning for a specific set of time via the optional seconds value.

Can also click the clock symbol either directly in chat or on the user badge which appears when clicking on a username.

To clear a timeout, either use the Unban command or overwrite the current timeout with a new, 1-second one.

/ban username

This command will allow you to permanently ban a user from the chat room.

Can also do this by clicking the Cancel symbol either directly in chat or on the user badge which appears when clicking on a username.

/unban username

This command will allow you to lift a permanent ban on a user from the chat room. You can also use this command to end a ban early; this also applies to timeouts.

Can also do this by clicking the Unban button which replaces the Ban button.

/slow seconds

This command allows you to set a limit on how often users in the chat room are allowed to send messages (rate limiting).

Twitch Partners with a Subscription Button can allow their Subscribers to bypass the slow mode filter if they wish to do so by going to their dashboard and navigating to their subscriptions tab.

/slowoff

This command allows you to disable slow mode if you had previously set it.

/followers

This command allows you or your mods to restrict chat to all or some of your followers, based on how long they’ve followed — from 0 minutes (all followers) to 3 months.

Here are a few example commands, which can be any time up to 3 months:

  • /followers 30m, or /followers 30 minutes
  • /followers 2h, or /followers 1 hours
  • /followers 2d, or /followers 2 days
  • /followers 1w, or /followers 1 week
  • /followers 3mo, or /followers 3 months

/followersoff

This command will disable followers only mode if it was previously enabled on the channel.

/subscribers

This command allows you to set your room so only users subscribed to you can talk in the chat room. If you don’t have the subscription feature it will only allow the Broadcaster and the channel moderators to talk in the chat room.

Subscriptions are a premium feature for select partners that require a paid purchase for the viewer to participate.

/subscribersoff

This command allows you to disable subscribers only chat room if you previously enabled it.

/clear

This command will allow the Broadcaster and chat moderators to completely wipe the previous chat history.

Users with IRC or browser add-ons may not see the chat get wiped due to history saving features and logging.

/requests

Opens the Channel Points requests queue to view and manage custom reward requests

/uniquechat

This command disallows users from posting non-unique messages to the channel. It will check for a minimum of 9 characters that are not symbol unicode characters and then purges any repetitive chat lines beyond that. Uniquechat is a unique way of moderating, which essentially allows you to stop generic copy-pasted messages intended as spam among over generally annoying content.

/uniquechatoff

This command will disable Uniquechat mode if it was previously enabled on the channel.

/emoteonly

This command allows you to set your room so only messages that are 100% emotes are allowed.

/emoteonlyoff

This command allows you to disable emote only mode if you previously enabled it.

/poll

Open a setup menu to create a poll.

/endpoll

End the active poll in the given channel

/deletepoll

Delete the active poll on the given channel

/commercial 30|60|90|120|150|180

Chat Command Error Troubleshooting

Commands you do not have permission to use will not appear when you try to enter them. For instance, if you are not a Moderator or Broadcaster, typing /shoutout [username] in a channel will result in the command disappearing.

If you misspell a command or use one that doesn’t exist, you’ll see an error Unrecognized Command in most instances.

For most other errors, the error message will include an explanation or solution.

Please contact Twitch Support here if you have further questions or need further assistance.

If you have a problem with a bot command we suggest reaching out directly to the bot’s developer, as Twitch Support will not be able to effectively troubleshoot third party products for you. Bots will usually use !commands, while Twitch native chat functions use /commands.

Chat Verification Settings

Chat Verification settings allow streamers to configure requirements that viewers must meet to chat in their channel. This article is for streamers managing their moderation settings.

Having trouble chatting? This article is for streamers setting up chat requirements. If you’re having trouble chatting or verifying your account:

  • Visit Why Can’t I Chat? for troubleshooting steps
  • Go to Security Settings to verify your email or phone number
  • See Managing Your Phone Number for verification issues

If a phone-verified or email-verified account is suspended site-wide or banned at the channel level, all accounts tied to that number or email will also be suspended and/or channel-banned. You also won’t be able to use that phone number/email to verify additional accounts if it is already tied to a suspended account.

To access these moderation settings, navigate to your Creator Dashboard, click Moderation, and then Settings (Moderation).

Email Verification

Email verification settings cover whether a user must have a verified email address to chat within your channel. We’ve broken this down into three possible choices while also providing granular options if you choose. Users attempting to chat in your channel that do not meet your set requirement will be prompted to verify their account and will then additionally be subject to any time based requirements (if set) before being allowed to send a chat message.

All chatters

This setting requires that all chatters must have a verified email address to chat within your channel with the exception of your set “Verification Exemption” settings.

Some chatters

This setting provides a few additional granular options that you can enable and configure to fit your needs. Any exempt groups in your “Verification Exemption” settings will not be impacted by these settings.

  • First-time chatters in my channel must have a verified email: If a user has not chatted in your channel prior to this option being enabled, they will be required to have a verified email address before being able to send a message in your channel.
  • Chatters without a verified email must have accounts older than [Option]: If a user does not have a verified email this option sets a requirement for how old their account must be for them to be able to chat. This setting allows you to configure how old their account must be, from a range of 1 hour to 6 months.
  • Chatters without a verified email must have followed for more than [Option]: If a user does not have a verified email this option sets a requirement for how long they must have been following your channel for them to be able to chat. This setting allows you to configure how long they must have been following, from a range of 10 Minutes to 3 months.
Email verification is off

This setting will disable the requirement of a verified email being required for chatters to chat in your channel.

Phone Verification

Phone verification settings cover whether a user must have a verified phone number to chat within your channel. We’ve broken this down into three possible choices while also providing granular options if you choose. Users attempting to chat in your channel that do not meet your set requirement will be prompted to verify their account and will then additionally be subject to any time based requirements (if set) before being allowed to send a chat message.

All chatters

This setting requires that all chatters must have a verified phone number to chat within your channel with the exception of your set “Verification Exemption” settings.

Some chatters

This setting provides a few additional granular options that you can enable and configure to fit your needs. Any exempt groups in your “Verification Exemption” settings will not be impacted by these settings.

  • First-time chatters in my channel must have a phone number: If a user has not chatted in your channel prior to this option being enabled, they will be required to have a verified phone number before being able to send a message in your channel.
  • Chatters without a verified phone number must have accounts older than [Option]: If a user does not have a verified phone number this option sets a requirement for how old their account must be for them to be able to chat. This setting allows you to configure how old their account must be, from a range of 1 hour to 6 months.
  • Chatters without a verified phone number must have followed for more than [Option]: If a user does not have a verified phone number this option sets a requirement for how long they must have been following your channel for them to be able to chat. This setting allows you to configure how long they must have been following, from a range of 10 Minutes to 3 months.
Phone number verification is off

This setting will disable the requirement of a verified phone number being required for chatters to chat in your channel.

Verification Exemption

Verification Exemption allows you to configure whether certain groups in your channel must meet the verification criteria you’ve set up. You may toggle exemptions for Subscribers, VIPs and Moderations of your channel.

Making an exemption for any of these groups will exempt them from having to meet any phone or email verification requirements.

Safety Rating

At the top of your Chat Verification settings you can find an indication of how we rate your overall safety rating based on the settings you’ve chosen.

If you’re unsure you can always use the preconfigured minimum settings we recommend by clicking the “Set All to Twitch minimum recommendation” button below your exemption list. This will provide you with a moderate safety rating and you can adjust to your preferences.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will this prevent malicious bots from entering my channel?
Botting is a longstanding, internet-wide problem that will never have an easy fix, but this added layer of account verification will certainly make it harder for malicious actors to spam-bot your channel en masse. No single tech solution will ever block bad actors’ behavior entirely, but this new hurdle will work within our constantly evolving suite of technologies and tooling, to slow them down considerably and reduce the number of channels they can impact. To make it even harder for bad actors to harass you through multiple accounts at once, we’ve designed the tool so that when one account tied to a verified phone number is suspended, all of the accounts are.
Will enabling this tool impact the discoverability or interactivity of my channel?
While users who aren’t phone verified may not be able to chat in your channel, this shouldn’t impact your discoverability, or the way that phone verified users can organically interact in chat. In fact, a key advantage to this tool is that it helps keep bad actors out of chat in the first place, so you won’t have to react to them with other measures that could have a bigger impact on your chat’s flow.

We’ve also designed the tool so that depending on your preferences, not all users must be phone verified to participate in chat. You can control settings so that only accounts of a certain age, following time, or chat history must be phone verified, and you can also exempt specific groups, like VIPs, Subscribers, and moderators.

Can I make an exception for a specific user if they’re not a Subscriber, VIP or Moderator in my channel?
Exceptions can only be made on a group level basis, if you’d like to provide a user with an exemption consider making them a VIP or Moderator within your channel and enabling a verification exemption for that group.
I’m a viewer and can’t chat because of verification requirements. What do I do?
This article is for streamers configuring their channel settings. If you’re having trouble chatting:
  • Visit your Security Settings to verify your email or phone number
  • See Why Can’t I Chat? for troubleshooting steps
  • If you’re having issues with verification codes or phone number errors, see Managing Your Phone Number
Why am I not receiving verification codes?
This article covers streamer settings, not verification troubleshooting. For help with verification codes, email delivery issues, or phone number problems, visit Managing Your Phone Number or contact Twitch Support.

GIF Keyboard on Twitch

Tier 2 and Tier 3 paid subscribers can send GIFs in chat using the GIF Keyboard, in channels where the streamer has this feature enabled. GIFs you send are subject to the same Community Guidelines and moderation tools as any other chat message.

Streamers: About GIF Keyboard

In channels where the streamer has enabled it, Tier 2 and Tier 3 paid subscribers can search for and post GIFs in chat. GIF Keyboard is available to all monetized streamers and is turned on by default. There is a 30-second cooldown before a user can send another GIF.

Turning GIF Keyboard On or Off

GIF Keyboard is on by default. To turn it off, go to your Monetization dashboard under Subscriptions and adjust your GIF settings.

Moderating and Reporting GIFs

GIF messages you send are subject to the Community Guidelines and can be moderated like any other chat message:

  • Streamers and moderators can delete individual GIF messages from chat
  • Set up to respect AutoMod settings: GIF search terms that match banned words or phrases will not show results
  • GIF messages respect limiting chat modes such as Emote-Only Mode, or Shield Mode
  • Timeouts and bans prevent users from sending GIFs, as with any chat message

GIF messages can be reported like any other chat message through the standard reporting process.

Viewers: How to Send GIF Messages

To send GIFs in chat, you must be a Tier 2 or Tier 3 paid subscriber in a channel with GIF keyboard enabled. Your account must not be timed out, banned, or otherwise restricted from chatting.

How to send a GIF message:

  • Select the Emote icon in chat

  • Choose the GIFs tab

  • Search or browse GIFs

  • Send it!

GIFs send as a single message and are subject to a 30-second cooldown between sends. GIF messages follow all channel moderation settings.

Considerations of GIF Use

GIFs you send are your responsibility. Your use of GIFs must comply with Twitch’s Community Guidelines and Terms of Service. GIFs are for use in chat; streamers that use GIFs in additional non-chat ways do so at their own risk.

About Violative GIF Use

If a user sends a GIF message that violates Twitch’s policies, they are held responsible. Related stream content (such as a livestream, VOD, or Clip) could be removed if the chat and violative GIF is shown on screen.

About GIF Content Ratings

The below content ratings are used by GIPHY to categorize GIFs in its catalog, and are not ratings defined or assigned by Twitch. All GIF use must comply with the Community Guidelines regardless of the channel’s content rating setting.

The GIF Keyboard on Twitch uses GIPHY’s content ratings to filter GIFs available in each channel:

  • PG (default): Suitable for most audiences. This is the default for all channels.
  • G: More restrictive, suitable for all ages.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can streamers upload content they own to the GIF keyboard on Twitch?
The GIF keyboard on Twitch utilizes GIPHY’s branded content library. Learn how to apply for a Brand channel with GIPHY here.
How can streamers moderate the volume of GIFs in chat?
By default, there is a 30-second cooldown between GIF messages sent, per user.
Why can’t I send GIFs?
You may not be able to send GIFs for one of these reasons:
  • You are not subscribed at Tier 2 or higher in this channel
  • The streamer has disabled GIF keyboard for their channel
  • The streamer is not a monetized channel, so GIF Keyboard is not available in their channel
  • The channel is in Emote-Only Mode, Shield Mode, or another mode that prevents GIF messages
  • You are timed out or banned from this channel’s chat
  • Your account has a chat restriction
Do GIF messages affect the viewing experience of users with older devices, or limited network quality?
Some older or incompatible devices may not see GIFs render in chat. In that case, those users will see the name of the GIF displayed in chat.
GIF messages should not add significant strain to viewing streams on a limited data connection. However, viewers can disable animations on Twitch via their chat appearance settings, to stop GIF movement in chat. With this setting enabled, a static preview of the GIF is displayed instead of a moving GIF.
What do I do if I see a GIF in my chat that I don’t like?
GIF messages can be moderated like any other chat message. Streamers and moderators can delete GIF messages and take moderation action against the sender. Additionally, GIF keyboard search terms are set up to respect AutoMod banned word settings — search terms that match blocked words or phrases will not produce results.
Viewers who wish to stop GIF message movement in chat altogether may disable animations via their chat appearance settings. Note that this setting only affects GIFs sent in chat via the GIF keyboard. GIFs on Twitch introduced via other methods, such as streamer overlay, may still appear.
